title: Haemorrhagic Transformation in Breakthrough Ischemic Stroke: Clinical Characteristics, Outcomes, and Anticoagulation Resumption Timing-Insights from the ASPERA-R Study.
journal: International journal of stroke : official journal of the International Stroke Society
abstract: The timing of anticoagulation resumption in patients who experience ischemic stroke despite ongoing anticoagulation and develop haemorrhagic transformation (HT) remains uncertain. We aimed to describe the characteristics and outcomes of patients with HT after a breakthrough ischemic stroke and to explore the association between anticoagulation resumption timing and the model-predicted balance of recurrent ischemic and bleeding risks in this high-risk population. We analysed data from patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke receiving anticoagulation therapy from the multicentre ASPERA-R registry. Analyses focused on patients with HT. HT was defined according to the Heidelberg Bleeding Classification based on brain imaging within 24 hours and categorized as haemorrhagic infarction (HI) or parenchymal hematoma (PH). Anticoagulation resumption and its timing were determined by treating clinicians and were not randomized. Landmark Cox regression models were used to evaluate recurrent ischemic events and moderate-to-severe bleeding after anticoagulation resumption. Restricted cubic spline models and exploratory net clinical benefit analyses integrating ischemic and bleeding risks were used to assess the relationship between anticoagulation resumption timing and model-predicted combined risk, overall and across clinically relevant subgroups. Among 1,555 patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke, 269 (17.3%) developed HT, of whom 170 (63.2%) resumed anticoagulation and contributed to the restart-timing analyses. At 90 days, patients with HT had higher crude rates of recurrent ischemic events (27.1% vs 13.8%), moderate-to-severe bleeding (7.4% vs 2.8%), and mortality (34.2% vs 17.7%) compared with patients without HT. In landmark analyses, HT was not associated with recurrent ischemic events (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.85-2.37) but remained strongly associated with moderate-to-severe bleeding (HR 3.39, 95% CI 1.61-7.13). Exploratory net clinical benefit analyses showed that the model-predicted combined risk reached its nadir at approximately 10 days after stroke in the overall HT population, with substantial uncertainty around this estimate. HT is a marker of poor prognosis in patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke, with an increased risk of bleeding after anticoagulation resumption. Among selected patients who resumed anticoagulation, exploratory modelling suggested that the combined predicted ischemic and bleeding risk reached its nadir at approximately 10 days after stroke. Given the non-randomized treatment timing and potential for treatment-selection bias, this estimate is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation.

title: Cell-specific transcription dysregulation in human Huntington's disease-positive developing striatum.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Progressive loss of striatal projection neurons leads to cognitive, psychiatric, and motor impairments that typically manifest in midlife, despite the expansion being present from conception. Increasing evidence supports a neurodevelopmental component to HD; however, authentic human developing HD-positive striatal tissue has not previously been characterised. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to compare an HD-positive human fetal striatal sample to an age- and sex-matched control, with CAG-repeat lengths of 16, 49 and 16, 17 respectively. We also compared the fetal HD-positive transcriptional signature with publicly available datasets from postmortem adult HD-positive brain tissue. We identified 2,032 differentially expressed genes and defined nine cellular clusters.. Gene enrichment analysis revealed alteration of key biological processes across the developing HD-positive striatum, with pathway-level dysregulation varying between clusters. There was substantial overlap in gene expression changes between fetal and adult HD-positive striatal tissues, although not in all transcriptional profiles, and some were reversed. Together, these findings demonstrate that molecular features of HD pathology are present during early human striatal development, supporting the concept that disease mechanisms are established decades prior to clinical onset.

title: Terminology for describing the 24-h cycle of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep: a scoping review.
journal: The international journal of behavioral nutrition and physical activity
abstract: Physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep are three behaviours which occupy the 24-h cycle and interact to influence a multitude of health outcomes. Different terms are currently used to describe these behaviours collectively (e.g., movement behaviours or physical behaviours). The lack of clear and consistent terminology makes it hard to compare, interpret, and build on research findings. As a first step towards developing consensus on what terminology to use for discussing the 24-h cycle of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep, we conducted a scoping review to identify the breadth of terminology used to describe this phenomenon. All searches occurred between September 18th - 20th 2024. We searched nine databases: Medline, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycInfo, Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, Education Source, and Compendex from inception to September 18th 2024. The Journal of Activity, Sedentary and Sleep Behaviors and the International Network of Time-Use Epidemiologists (INTUE) publication lists were manually searched on September 19th - 20th 2024. Peer-reviewed articles were included if they 1) were published in English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Chinese, Korean, or Japanese; 2) focused on humans; and 3) describe physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep in an integrated manner. We identified different terminologies used for collectively discussing physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep across the 24-h cycle. Our search identified 10,749 articles of which 979 articles met our inclusion criteria. Across all articles, 199 different terms were used to describe physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep collectively. The term movement behaviours was used in 673 articles, 24-h movement behaviours was used in 457 articles, physical behaviours was used in 58 articles, 24-h activity cycle was used in 36 articles, and time-use behaviours was used in 31 articles. The two most popular terms for describing the collective interaction of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep are movement behaviours and 24-h movement behaviours. However, there is not yet an internationally recognized and agreed-upon term for holistically describing the 24-h cycle of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep. Developing a homogeneous and widely accepted set of terminology and definitions is thus critical if we hope to ensure clarity, enhance reproducibility, and enable the translation of future research into coherent guidelines, policies, and practices for these behaviours.

title: Repurposing thioridazine as a novel treatment for melanoma brain metastasis.
abstract: A substantial proportion of patients with melanoma brain metastases (MBM), especially those symptomatic at therapy start, continue to respond poorly to currently available systemic therapies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors. Durable systemic treatment options beyond established regimens remain limited for this patient population. Drug repurposing offers a rapid translational path for identifying novel therapeutic strategies. Thioridazine, a phenothiazine antipsychotic with known blood-brain barrier permeability, has shown anticancer effects in several malignancies but has not previously been evaluated in MBM. This study investigates the anti-tumoral potential and underlying mechanisms of thioridazine in patient-derived MBM cell lines. Cytotoxic, anti-proliferative, and anti-migratory effects of thioridazine were assessed in four MBM cell lines (H1, H2, H3, H10) using monolayer and soft agar viability assays, live-cell imaging, and clonogenic assays. Potential off-target toxicity was evaluated using fetal rat brain organoids (FRBOs). Mechanistic effects were examined using Annexin V/PI flow cytometry, Western blotting of apoptosis- and autophagy-related proteins (cleaved PARP1, cleaved caspase-3, Bcl-2, p62, LC3A/B), and confocal microscopy to assess autophagosome formation and lysosomal dynamics. Thioridazine reduced viability of MBM cells in a dose-dependent manner, with IC50 values ranging from 8.7 to 12.0 µM. Anchorage-independent growth was similarly inhibited. FRBOs displayed no treatment-associated cytotoxicity at MBM-relevant doses in vitro. Thioridazine markedly suppressed MBM cell proliferation, migration, and clonogenic growth in a dose-dependent manner. Apoptosis induction was inconsistent across cell lines, with variable activation of cleaved PARP1, cleaved caspase-3, and Bcl-2. In contrast, autophagy-associated markers p62 and LC3A/B were consistently upregulated, accompanied by intracellular accumulation of punctate autophagosomes and altered lysosomal morphology, indicating impaired autophagic flux. Thioridazine demonstrates robust anti-tumoral activity in MBM cells in vitro while sparing healthy brain organoid tissue. Its cytotoxic effects appear independent of classical apoptosis and instead correlate with disrupted autophagic flux and altered lysosomal dynamics. These findings highlight thioridazine as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing in MBM and support further investigation into its autophagy-modulating mechanisms.

title: Social determinants of health and lifestyle in the progression of degenerative bone and joint diseases: a prospective multi-state analysis.
abstract: The role of social determinants of health (SDOH) in the progression of degenerative bone and joint diseases (DBJDs) - from initial onset to multimorbidity and mortality - remains unclear. We aimed to assess the associations of SDOH with DBJDs progression, examine the mediating role of lifestyle, and explore their joint effects. A total of 283,146 participants from the UK Biobank were included. SDOH was constructed using 17 items including economic, education, healthcare, neighbourhood, and social domains, and categorized into favourable, intermediate, and unfavourable groups. The outcomes of interest were first DBJD (FDBJD), DBJM (the coexistence of at least two DBJDs), and all-cause mortality. Multi-state models were employed to estimate risks across five disease transitions. During a median follow-up of 13.7 years, 43,172 participants developed FDBJD, of whom, 4,170 subsequently developed DBJM, and 18,831 died. Compared with favourable SDOH, unfavourable SDOH was associated with increased risks of all transitions, including from baseline to FDBJD (HR = 1.21, 95%CI = 1.18-1.24), from baseline to death (1.58 [1.52-1.65]), from FDBJD to DBJM (1.33 [1.23-1.44]), from FDBJD to death (1.64 [1.50-1.80]), and from DBJM to death (1.48 [1.17-1.87]). Economic stability and social and community context emerged as the most robust predictors. Lifestyle factors partially mediated the associations, with proportions of mediation ranging from 2.47% to 10.77%. Participants with unfavourable SDOH and lifestyle exhibited the highest risks, with significant additive interactions observed in transitions of death from baseline or after FDBJD. Unfavourable SDOH are strongly associated with progression and mortality of DBJDs, with effects that extend beyond individual lifestyle factors. These findings underscore the importance of addressing upstream social determinants, alongside lifestyle promotion, to reduce the burden of DBJDs and social inequalities in musculoskeletal health.

title: Facilitators and barriers to the early implementation of speaking valves in intensive care: a qualitative study using normalisation process theory.
abstract: The utilization of tracheostomy in conjunction with mechanical ventilation significantly impacts various physiological functions, particularly the ability to communicate verbally. Speaking valves, integrated into the ventilator circuit, restore phonation and are recognised internationally as best practice, yet remain underused in Swedish intensive care units (ICUs). Beyond enabling verbal communication, the early use of speaking valves has been associated with improved swallowing, secretion management, and reduced duration of mechanical ventilation. The TRACH INSPIRE project aims to promote their implementation in Swedish ICUs. This study explored facilitators and barriers to the early interprofessional implementation of speaking valves in tracheostomised, mechanically ventilated ICU patients. This qualitative study design analysed 19 semi-structured interview data, pre-implementation, with ICU professionals (intensivists, nurses, physiotherapists, and speech-language pathologists) from two participating ICUs in the TRACH INSPIRE project conducted in January-February 2025. Inclusion criteria were that the participants must have participated in the interprofessional competency training for the TRACH INSPIRE project. No formal exclusion criteria were defined. The Data were analysed using deductive content analysis guided by the Normalisation Process Theory (NPT), which examines how new practices are embedded into routine care. Twelve subcategories were identified that were organized according to the NPT. Facilitators included a shared understanding of the intervention's value, strong professional commitment, structured implementation processes, managerial support, clearly defined roles, effective interprofessional collaboration, targeted training, and open communication. Barriers centred on organisational constraints such as limited resources, low patient volumes, lack of a comprehensive implementation strategy, and documentation-related challenges. Early implementation of speaking valves in mechanically ventilated, tracheostomised ICU patients is supported by high interprofessional engagement, shared recognition of benefits, and structured training. However, operational limitations, small eligible patient populations, and documentation burdens present notable challenges. Inclusive team strategies, maintaining competencies, and streamlined processes may promote sustainable integration into routine ICU practice.

title: PN6047 demonstrates preclinical efficacy in headache models as a novel delta-opioid receptor agonist.
journal: The journal of headache and pain
abstract: The Delta-opioid receptor (DOR) has gained attention as a promising target for the treatment of migraine and headache disorders. This is largely attributed to its unique pharmacological profile, which suggests that DOR-targeting treatment offers effective therapeutic effect with a lower risk of medication-overuse headache (MOH), reduced abuse liability, and minimal potential for physical dependence. These advantages have driven the development of a novel DOR agonist PN6047 (3-[[4-(dimethylcarbamoyl) phenyl]-[1-(thiazol-5-ylmethyl)-4-piperidylidene] methyl]benzamide), which has completed Phase I clinical trial and showed a favorable safety and tolerability profile. Although PN6047 has shown promising effects in neuropathic pain models, its efficacy in preclinical models of headache-associated pain remains to be evaluated. Here, we investigated the effects of PN6047 in models of migraine-associated pain and aura as well as post-traumatic headache (PTH) and MOH. C57BL/6J mice were used to examine the effects of PN6047 in the following migraine models: chronic intermittent nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced migraine-associated pain, PTH, KCl-induced cortical spreading depression (CSD), and optogenetic evoked CSD in freely behaving transgenic mice expressing ChR2-eYFP. In addition, we tested whether chronic PN6047 induced MOH and whether it could prevent the development of MOH induced by sumatriptan. A single injection of PN6047 blocked chronic cephalic allodynia established by chronic intermittent NTG and PTH. Moreover, chronic PN6047 treatment prevented the development of MOH induced by sumatriptan, without causing MOH itself. In addition, PN6047 significantly reduced the number of CSD events in the KCl-induced CSD model, and delayed CSD onset triggered in freely behaving mice along with subsequent CSD-evoked allodynia. PN6047, a novel DOR agonist, attenuates headache-associated mechanisms and symptoms in preclinical models of chronic migraine, migraine aura, PTH, and MOH. Importantly, prolonged PN6047 treatment did not induce MOH or analgesic tolerance. Together, these data demonstrate that despite the distinct mechanisms underlying migraine and headache disorder models, PN6047 exhibits significant efficacy without inducing MOH, and displays a favorable safety and tolerability profile. Not applicable.

title: Role of gut microbiota dysbiosis on the functional outcomes in ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke patients: a systematic review.
abstract: Stroke is a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, yet the biological determinants of post-stroke recovery remain incompletely understood. Recent evidence implicates the gut microbiome as a key regulator of neuroinflammation, metabolic signalling, and immune response through microbiota-gut brain axis. However, the extent to which gut microbial dysbiosis influences neurological severity and functional recovery across ischemic and haemorrhagic stroke remains unclear. This systematic review examined the relationship between gut dysbiosis and functional outcomes following stroke. A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and the Cochrane Library identified eligible studies published up to July 2025. Twenty-three clinical studies comprising 2,951 participants were included. Microbiome diversity indices, microbial taxa, and microbiota-derived metabolites were evaluated in relation to standardized stroke outcomes, including acute neurological severity (NIHSS) and functional outcomes (mRS, Barthel Index. The study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and the Cochrane risk-of-bias framework. Across the included cohorts, stroke patients exhibited consistent alterations in gut microbial ecology compared with healthy controls. Alpha diversity analyses demonstrated a significant reduction in microbial richness and evenness in several cohorts, while beta diversity metrics revealed pronounced restructuring and clear separation between stroke and control microbiomes. Differential abundance analysis consistently identified depletion of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing commensals, including Roseburia, Faecalibacterium, and Coprococcus, alongside enrichment of opportunistic and pro-inflammatory taxa such as Enterobacteriaceae, Enterococcus, and Escherichia/Shigella. Metabolomic analysis further revealed a convergent disruption of key microbial metabolic pathways, including reduced SCFA production, increased endotoxin-associated signalling and trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) metabolism. These microbial and metabolic perturbations were significantly associated with greater neurological severity, higher disability scores, increased infection risk, and poorer functional outcomes following stroke. This systematic synthesis demonstrates that stroke is accompanied by a reproducible pattern of gut microbial dysbiosis characterized by ecological contraction, expansion of inflammatory pathobionts, and disruption of microbial metabolic signalling. These findings support the existence of a conserved gut-brain-metabolic axis influencing stroke severity and recovery trajectories. Integrating microbiome-derived biomarkers with clinical prognostic models may enable earlier risk stratification and the development of microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies to improve post-stroke outcomes. PROSPERO (Identifier: CRD420251106958).

title: Author Correction: Social rank modulates methamphetamine-seeking in dominant and subordinate male rodents via distinct dopaminergic pathways.
Head-mounted camera for reconstructing outdoor behavior in freely flying birds.
abstract: Capturing the fine details of behavior when animals perform complex tasks, such as prey pursuit and capture, in natural environments is a challenging endeavor. For birds of prey, commonly used tracking approaches, such as lightweight GPS and inertial measurement units, cannot simultaneously track the bird's position and the fine details of body part motion or moving external objects. Here we designed a head-mounted, tetherless, 4π camera system which, combined with a high-resolution environmental scan, enabled detailed three-dimensional measurement of both head position and orientation in freely flying Harris's hawks (Parabuteo unicinctus) performing aerial pursuit in the wild. This stable head-mounted imaging approach enabled reconstruction of flight trajectories in natural environments, detailed quantification of head motion, optic flow and target position, while the bird tracked and captured airborne targets.

title: TERRA: an induced responder to telomere dysfunction.
abstract: Telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) has long been viewed as a constitutive component of telomeres. However, accumulating experimental evidence suggests that TERRA is instead a stress-responsive signal produced specifically at dysfunctional telomeres. Across yeasts and mammals, TERRA abundance changes as telomeres shorten or become damaged, engaging the appropriate maintenance pathway through interactions with shelterin, chromatin regulators and DNA repair factors, and through the controlled formation of RNA:DNA hybrids (R-loops). In telomerase-negative cells, transient accumulation of TERRA and R-loops promotes homology-directed telomere elongation. In telomerase-positive cells, TERRA appears to direct telomerase activity selectively toward short telomeres. When telomere damage remains unresolved, sustained TERRA expression and persistent R-loops drive cells toward senescence, inflammatory signaling and crisis-associated cell death. We propose here that TERRA functions as a molecular rheostat at damaged telomeres: transient and spatially controlled induction restores chromosome-end integrity, whereas persistent accumulation results in the removal of compromised cells from the proliferative pool. Defining how cells set these switch points will be essential for elucidating how TERRA shapes ageing and disease and for harnessing its therapeutic potential.

title: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors.
abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes remains a critical challenge in oncology, in particular for childhood brain tumors, in which treatment decisions need to carefully balance risk of tumor recurrence and death against severe therapy-induced sequelae. Here, we developed MANTIS (methylation profiling and artificial neural networks for time-dependent individualized survival predictions), a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients. MANTIS generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. Extending MANTIS to estimate individualized treatment effects identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage (P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes. In conclusion, our study establishes a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in childhood brain tumors and offers a blueprint for similar initiatives in other cancer types.

title: TAAR5 Pharmacology.
abstract: Trace amine-associated receptor 5 (TAAR5) belongs to the TAAR family of G protein-coupled receptors, which detect trace amines, small molecules structurally related to monoamine neurotransmitters but present at much lower concentrations in vertebrate and invertebrate tissues. In both humans and rodents, TAAR5 is predominantly expressed in the olfactory epithelium, with lower expression also observed in the central nervous system. As an odorant receptor, TAAR5 is the principal mediator of trimethylamine sensing, an odor that is aversive in humans but has a crucial social function in mice. Accumulating evidence indicates that TAAR5 modulates serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmission within the central nervous system and is involved in affective, cognitive, and sensorimotor behaviors. More recently, TAAR5 has been implicated in a microbiota-derived trimethylamine signaling axis associated with circadian regulation. This chapter reviews the key studies that have shaped the current understanding of TAAR5, from its discovery to its involvement in complex central nervous system and behavioral processes.

title: Vasomechanic treatment is associated with increased efflux of human brain proteins.
abstract: An age-related neurovascular impairment in nitric oxide (NO)-mediated vasodilation and reciprocal Piezo1-dependent vascular vasoconstriction may precede the accumulation of soluble brain proteins such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and disruption of brain fluid homeostasis in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Preclinical studies suggest that restoring these pathways can enhance neurofluid transport and improve cognitive outcomes. In this study (EudraCT 2021-000625-27), we investigated the effects of sublingual NO and Piezo1-targeted whole-body vibrations (WBVp) in healthy adults (n = 29) using multimodal neuroimaging and blood biomarker analysis. The combined intervention (NO+WBVp) was associated with correlating changes in brain fluid dynamics and increased blood levels of soluble brain-derived proteins (Aβ40&42, GFAP). These effects increased with age and the magnitude of NO-induced hypotension. The interventions were well tolerated under controlled experimental conditions. Overall, the findings are consistent with transient redistribution of brain-derived proteins toward circulation, suggesting a potential non-invasive approach to increase neurofluidic solute efflux in humans. Pre-specified primary endpoints, changes in circulating brain-derived protein concentrations, brain fluid imaging and brain pulsation measures, were met. Secondary outcomes included physiological analyses.

title: Ca2+ signature gates responsiveness to exogenous auxin in Arabidopsis roots.
abstract: Plants must continually balance growth with arrest, especially under stress. Auxin signaling acts as a central regulatory hub in this process, yet the mechanisms that dynamically tune auxin signaling in real time remain unknown. Here, we use the light-gated, Ca2+-permeable Channelrhodopsin 2 variant XXM2.0 to optogenetically impose defined Ca2+ signatures on Arabidopsis root cells. Repetitive light activation triggers cytosolic Ca2+ signals that in turn suppress membrane depolarization and Ca2+ transients triggered by exogenous auxin. Moreover, prolonged optogenetic Ca2+ stimulation affects auxin-responsive transcriptional reprogramming. As phenotypic output, reversible inhibition of root growth by suppressing cell division and elongation is observed. We further identify a candidate CaM7-CNGC14 module that likely mediates Ca2+-dependent gating of responsiveness to exogenous auxin as well as Ca2+-dependent root growth inhibition. Our study thus introduces a synthetic biology approach to decompose calcium-auxin crosstalk in plant cells, and demonstrates that optogenetically imposed cytosolic Ca2+ signals act as dynamic regulators of auxin susceptibility in roots.

title: The postsynaptic scaffolding protein SAPAP3 shapes mitochondrial activity: the case of Huntington's disease.
abstract: Postsynaptic scaffolding protein SAP90/PSD95-associated protein 3 (SAPAP3) modulates cortico-striatal signalling and regulates the maintenance of synaptic structure. Notably, SAPAP3 defects have been reported in several human psychiatric disorders that share pathophysiological features with Huntington's disease (HD), a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the expression of mutant huntingtin (mHTT) and marked dysfunction of cortico-striatal synapses and mitochondria. However, the role of SAPAP3 in mitochondrial function and HD pathophysiology remains unexplored. SAPAP3 was extracted from striatal synaptoneurosomes and analyzed by SWATH-MS proteomics to identify potential interactors, revealing SAPAP3 association with several mitochondrial proteins, particularly Mic60. These data were further complemented with proximity ligation assay (PLA) and immunoprecipitation experiments, supporting a direct or indirect interaction between SAPAP3 and Mic60. SAPAP3 knockout (SAPAP3-KO) mouse striatum exhibited reduced Mic60 protein levels, decreased mitochondrial respiratory chain activity and Ca2+ uptake, as well as increased mitochondrial roundness and circularity, accompanied by decreased perimeter and area, consistent with mitochondrial fragmentation. Analysis of SAPAP3 protein levels in postmortem caudate tissue from HD patients, striatal tissue and isolated mitochondria from YAC128 mice, as well as mitochondria in primary striatal YAC128 neurons and STHdh Q111 cells, showed consistently reduced SAPAP3 levels. HD cells and WT cells subjected to SAPAP3 silencing showed alterations in mitochondrial morphology, movement and function. In contrast, HD striatal cells transfected with ovSAPAP3 constructs to restore SAPAP3 levels showed a rescue of mitochondrial morphology, motility, function and Ca2+ handling, together with decreased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These findings uncover a novel role for postsynaptic scaffolding protein SAPAP3 in preserving mitochondrial health, particularly mitochondrial dynamics and function, under neuropathological conditions characterized by mitochondrial abnormalities such as HD.

title: Conventional transcutaneous spinal stimulation waveforms recruit sensory pathways more effectively than burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms.
abstract: Transcutaneous spinal stimulation (TSS) can improve motor function in people with paresis, although outcomes remain inconsistent across studies. Different stimulation parameters may influence the effectiveness and sensory fiber selectivity of TSS. Here, we systematically compared the ability of ten TSS waveforms applied over the T11-L1 vertebral levels to evoke a soleus muscle response in people with intact neurological function (n = 12). Burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms (2 kHz, 5 kHz, 10 kHz) were compared with a conventional square waveform of the same total cathodal phase duration (400 μ s); a longer conventional waveform (1,000 μ s) was also tested. All waveforms were delivered in biphasic and monophasic pulse types. Relative to the conventional 400 μ s waveform, response threshold intensities were lower with the 1,000 μ s waveform (-28 to -27%) and higher with high-frequency stimulation: 2 kHz (+26 to +43%), 5 kHz (+111 to +129%), and 10 kHz (+254 to +273%). Recruitment curve slopes were also steeper with the 1,000 μ s waveform (+33 to +46%) and generally less steep with high-frequency stimulation: 2 kHz (biphasic: -25%), 5 kHz (-50 to -46%), and 10 kHz (-75 to -64%). Paired-pulse depression was weak at intensities >100%-120% of threshold but increased markedly at higher intensities across all waveforms. The 10 kHz waveforms showed the weakest paired-pulse depression, consistent with a smaller sensory contribution than the conventional 400 μ s waveform. Onset latencies were comparable to peripheral conduction times at near-threshold intensities but became shorter at higher stimulation intensities, suggesting changes in the relative contributions of sensory and motor fiber activation. Overall, burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms required higher stimulation intensities than conventional waveforms to evoke spinally-evoked motor responses and provided no physiological evidence of an advantage over conventional waveforms.

title: Spatially Resolved Cell-Fate Engineering through Nanoneedle-Mediated Optoporation.
abstract: The development of advanced tissue models demands spatially resolved control over cell fate to provide deeper insights into complex biological processes, yet precise intracellular manipulation remains a critical bottleneck in cellular engineering strategies. Current approaches for gene delivery struggle in achieving the required localized resolution to control individual cell fate, while optogenetic approaches are constrained by the requirement for complex genetic engineering and limited modes of gene regulation. Here, we show that nanoneedle-mediated optoporation enables spatially resolved intracellular delivery of nucleic acids, locally directing cell fate. Through computational modeling and experimental validation, we investigated the dependence of electromagnetic field enhancement on wavelength, nanoneedle geometry, and porosity. We demonstrated the importance of surface chemistry for optoporation efficiency, achieving optimal transfection performance through thermal carbonization. This approach achieves efficient delivery for propidium iodide, 500 kDa dextran, and siRNA, alongside a 72% mRNA transfection efficiency, resulting in sustained protein expression after 24 h. Selective SNAIL1 mRNA transfection demonstrated localized cell-fate engineering, inducing a targeted epithelial to mesenchymal transition. This porous nanoneedle system presents a versatile and flexible approach for precise genetic manipulation through electromagnetic field tunability, offering new possibilities for studying complex biological processes and disease progression through spatially resolved control of cell fate.

title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
abstract: For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural-behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network.
abstract: Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. 'Autonomic imbalance' between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

title: Tau positron emission tomography imaging in progressive supranuclear palsy: A review of phenotypes, symptoms, and clinical severity.
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is an atypical parkinsonian four tandem-repeat (4R) tauopathy, predominantly affecting subcortical and brainstem regions, with later cortical involvement. PSP is frequently misdiagnosed, highlighting the need for reliable biomarkers for accurate diagnosis and assessing clinical severity. Tau positron emission tomography (PET) has emerged as a potential tool for detecting 4R tau in vivo. This review summarizes current evidence on tau PET imaging in PSP, focusing on diagnostic differentiation, clinical phenotypes, symptoms, and disease severity. A literature search was conducted using PubMed and Google Scholar for studies on tau PET imaging in PSP, including 4R tau pathology and first- and second-generation tau PET tracers. We focused on evidence of regional tracer uptake across diagnoses and PSP phenotypes and associations with clinical symptoms and disease severity. Tau PET demonstrates regional uptake patterns that may differentiate PSP from other tauopathies, clinically similar disorders, and PSP phenotypes. Regional uptake has the potential for characterizing motor and non-motor features, including balance, speech, oculomotor function, cognitive and behavioural changes, sleep disturbances and autonomic dysfunction. However, interpretation remains limited by off-target binding, variable 4R tau affinity, methodological variabilities, and inconsistent correspondence with post-mortem tau burden. Tau PET shows potential as a biomarker for diagnosis, clinical characterization, and disease monitoring in PSP, although current limitations restrict its clinical utility. More selective 4R tau tracers, longitudinal studies, PET-to-autopsy validations, further correlations with clinical scales, and standardized PET analysis methods are needed to establish its utility for monitoring disease progression and prognosis.

title: A Water Compartment Cell Culture Lid Enables Stable Longitudinal Recording of Neuronal Networks In Vitro.
abstract: Longitudinal electrophysiological recordings of neuronal networks are essential for studying network maturation, plasticity, and pharmacological responses. Yet, current microelectrode array (MEA) approaches are limited by evaporation-induced drift in culture conditions, exacerbated by heat dissipation from active recording electronics on CMOS-based high-density MEAs. We present a cell culture lid featuring a water compartment at its interface that eliminates evaporation whilst maintaining gas exchange. Combined with a custom incubator that uses independent temperature control of the MEA to prevent condensation, the system enables stable, uninterrupted recordings for weeks. We show that perturbations in firing rate and functional connectivity following medium exchange are significantly reduced by suppressing evaporation. We demonstrate continuous 35-day recordings of patterned human iPSC-derived neuronal networks with a single half-medium exchange, revealing multiple spatiotemporal firing patterns that are held concurrently and evolve over weeks. All design files are provided, enabling adoption across culturing platforms for longitudinal studies of development within individual cultures, and establishing the conditions required for studies of plasticity and chronic pharmacology.

title: Physiological Representation of Social Evaluation: Modeling Human Eye Movements, Pupillary, and Neuronal Responses to Faces.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Face-based social evaluations are ubiquitous and consequential, yet it remains unclear how these evaluations are represented in spontaneous physiological responses. Across four studies (222 participants: 142 females, 57 males, 23 unreported; 503 neurons), we used a data-driven modeling framework to examine how facial appearance shapes eye movements, pupillary responses, and neuronal activity during face viewing. We asked what these responses reveal about the underlying social evaluations. Pupillary responses and hippocampal firing during saccades were driven by facial variation associated with an integrated combination of valence and power evaluations; fixation duration on the eyes and hippocampal firing during fixations were more selectively tuned to threat-related evaluations; amygdalar firing primarily tracked approachability-related valence. A prospective validation study confirmed that novel faces synthesized along these modeled directions elicited the predicted physiological responses in new participants. We also found evidence of individual differences: social anxiety selectively heightened the sensitivity of pupillary responses to face evaluations. These findings suggest that distinct physiological responses across attention, autonomic arousal, and medial temporal lobe activity reflect distinct but related facets of face-based social evaluation.Significance Statement Everyday social decisions hinge on split-second impressions of unfamiliar faces. When we see a face, we instantly judge the person's likely intention (positive ↔ negative valence) and social influence (high ↔ low power). Across four complementary studies, we show that these evaluative processes are reflected in physiological responses to faces across overt attention, autonomic arousal, and subcortical neuronal firing. Different physiological systems reflected partially distinct but related facets of social-evaluative meaning, including integrated valence-and-power, threat-related, and approachability-related evaluation.

title: Multiple combinations of GPCR activation gate the induction of NMDAR-independent LTD in mouse visual cortex.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Activity-dependent synaptic weakening, including long-term depression (LTD), is a fundamental mechanism underlying experience-dependent circuit remodeling. At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of LTD have been identified: NMDAR-LTD, triggered by activation of NMDA receptors, and mGluR-LTD, mediated by group I metabotropic glutamate receptors. NMDAR-LTD is the best-characterized form and has been described in numerous brain regions. In contrast, in cortical synapses mGluR-LTD has been investigated primarily in the hippocampus, where it requires mGluR5 activation and its molecular mechanisms are well established. Although NMDAR-LTD is also well documented in the neocortex, mGluR-LTD remains comparatively poorly characterized, particularly in primary sensory cortices, despite growing evidence that mGluR signaling contributes to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. We examined mGluR-LTD in slices of primary visual cortex of rats and mice of all sexes and found that layer II/III pyramidal neurons do express an NMDAR-independent LTD. Like in CA1, mGluR-LTD in V1 depends on mGluR5 activation and ongoing protein synthesis regulated by FMRP. Unlike CA1, however, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in V1 requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This more stringent gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with the view that the hippocampus and neocortex are specialized for rapid and gradual learning, respectively.Significance statement At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of long-term depression (LTD) have been identified: NMDAR-LTD and mGluR-LTD. While NMDAR-LTD is widespread, mGluR-LTD has been studied primarily in the hippocampus and remains poorly characterized in sensory cortices, despite evidence that mGluRs contribute to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. This study shows that an NMDAR-independent form of LTD can be induced in visual cortical slices. Unlike hippocampus, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in visual cortex requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This stricter gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with its role in gradual, rather than rapid, learning.

title: Learning-dependent hippocampal-striatal reorganization during sequential decision-making in pigeons.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Adaptive sequential decision-making requires animals to learn how actions shape future states and rewards while adjusting behavioral strategies as experience accumulates. Although the hippocampus is implicated in state-structure representation and the striatum in value learning, how learning strategies evolve from exploratory sampling to efficient exploitation and how hippocampal-striatal interactions reorganize alongside this transition remain unclear. We trained six pigeons of undetermined sex to perform a probabilistic two-step decision task while simultaneously recording behavioral choices and hippocampal-striatal local field potentials. Strategy evolution was tracked using a dynamic reinforcement-learning framework in which model-based, model-free, and weighted model-based/model-free models were fitted across sliding windows. Hippocampal-striatal functional coordination was assessed using phase-locking analysis, and directed predictive influence was quantified using kernel Granger causality. The weighted model best explained choice dynamics, indicating a shift from model-based-like control during early acquisition toward model-free-like control during later stable performance. This behavioral shift was accompanied by two complementary neural changes: hippocampal-striatal phase coordination increased across learning, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased and covaried positively with model-based-like strategy weight. Direction-ratio analysis showed that hippocampus-to-striatum remained the predominant direction throughout learning, indicating reduced influence rather than directional reversal. After acquisition, hippocampus-to-striatum directed influence was not uniformly reduced but remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, unrewarded, or less expected events. Together, these findings reveal a learning-dependent reorganization of hippocampal-striatal dynamics, in which increasing functional coordination is accompanied by reduced but condition-dependent hippocampal-to-striatal influence as behavior becomes more stable and efficient.Significance Statement Adaptive learning requires coordinated changes in behavioral strategy and neural interactions as animals progress from exploration to stable performance. Here, we show that pigeons gradually shifted from flexible, model-based-like control toward more stable, model-free-like behavior during sequential learning. In parallel, hippocampal-striatal interactions underwent a complementary reorganization: phase coordination progressively increased, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased with declining model-based-like control. Importantly, this directed influence remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, or unrewarded events. These findings link behavioral strategy transition to the dynamic reorganization of hippocampal-striatal interactions, revealing how neural systems may simultaneously support efficient learned behavior while retaining sensitivity to behaviorally informative events.

title: Opioid-glutamate interactions modulate intrinsically rewarded communication in European starlings.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is essential for social learning and bonding, yet relatively little is known about its neural bases. Past research on songbirds demonstrates that song produced in affiliative, non-sexual flocks correlates positively with a bird's intrinsic reward state, and the link between song and reward is regulated by mu opioid receptors (MORs) in the medial preoptic area (MPOA). RNAseq studies also reveal a strong positive association between affiliative song and glutamatergic gene expression in MPOA, with NMDA receptor 1 (GRIN1) and glutamate receptor scaffolding protein (Shank2) correlating strongly with affiliative singing. In male European starlings we tested the hypothesis that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA regulate affiliative communication. Peripheral administration of the MOR agonist fentanyl increased affiliative singing and calling behavior while reducing stress-related behavior, beak wiping. The effects on vocal but not stress-related behavior were prevented by administration of the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801. c-Fos mapping revealed that fentanyl increased neural activity in caudal MPOA (cMPOA) and interconnected regions implicated in social behavior, song production, and reward, and that these effects were reversed by MK-801. To identify a local site of MOR-glutamate interaction, we used AAV shRNA to downregulate Shank2 in MPOA. This manipulation prevented fentanyl from stimulating affiliative singing behavior, also without affecting stress reduction, suggesting that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA facilitate social communication but not associated stress reduction. Together these findings provide the first experimental evidence that MOR-glutamate interactions within the MPOA, particularly the cMPOA, contribute to affiliative, rewarding vocal communication.Significance Statement Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is fundamental to social cohesion and well-being, yet its neural mechanisms are poorly understood. This study identifies a critical role for interactions between mu opioid receptors and glutamatergic signaling in promoting non-sexual, rewarding vocal communication. In a songbird experimental system, we demonstrate that NMDA receptor activity and the postsynaptic glutamate receptor scaffolding protein Shank2 are required for opioid facilitation of affiliative song. Our findings further reveal the medial preoptic area, particularly its caudal subdivision, to be an important site of this opioid-glutamate interaction. Together, these results extend opioid-glutamate interaction frameworks beyond classic reward circuits and suggest the existence of a conserved neural mechanism supporting affiliative social behavior across vertebrates.

title: Mitochondria-Associated Membranes as a Convergent Hub of Brain Aging: From Neurodegeneration to Cerebral Ischemia.
abstract: Brain aging is the principal risk factor for both neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) and cerebral ischemic disorders, yet the subcellular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely defined. Mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs)-specialized contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondria-sit at the intersection of two well-established hallmarks of aging, mitochondrial dysfunction, and loss of proteostasis, making them an attractive mechanistic node for understanding age-related brain decline. In this review, we propose a MAM-centered framework that unifies neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathology under the broader paradigm of brain aging. We first summarize the molecular architecture of MAMs and their core functions in neuronal Ca2+ transfer, mitochondrial dynamics, lipid metabolism, inflammasome assembly, and autophagic quality control, together with emerging evidence from non-neuronal brain cells. We then examine how MAM dysfunction intersects with five hallmarks of aging-mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and altered intercellular communication-drawing on evidence from physiological aging and cellular senescence models. Next, we discuss disease-specific roles of MAMs in cerebral ischemia and in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. A central theme emerges: Rather than a unidirectional decline of MAMs, brain aging is associated with a loss of MAM homeostasis, in which both insufficient and excessive ER-mitochondria coupling can be pathological and the shared deficit is the failure to maintain contact-site function within an optimal range. Finally, we consider age-relevant therapeutic and biomarker strategies targeting MAMs and their potential translation into geriatric neurology. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate MAM biology across physiological brain aging, cerebral ischemia, and the four major NDDs within a single homeostatic framework, offering a unified perspective on the mechanisms of age-related brain decline.

title: An exploratory investigation of speech-in-noise ability and cognitive performance in young adult contact sport athletes.
abstract: To explore speech-in-noise abilities and cognitive performance in young adult contact sport athletes exposed to repetitive head impacts (RHI). An exploratory cross-sectional study using standardized speech-in-noise and neuropsychological assessments alongside self-reported sporting history, listening‑in‑noise ability, and concussion history as proxy indicators of exposure. Twenty-four athletes (17 females, 7 males; median age 20 years, range 18-29 years) actively participating in the contact sport of rugby union in Sheffield, UK. Elevated rates of impairment relative to normative expectations were observed on the Listening in Spatialized Noise-Sentences (LiSN-S) High Cue (30.8%) and Low Cue (38.5%) tests and the Trail Making Test (TMT) A (19.2%) and B (73.1%). Low rates of impairment were observed on the LiSN-S Total Advantage test (3.8%), the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (3.8%) and the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test trials (0%) and long delay (3.8%). Statistically significant (p < 0.01) group-level Z-score deviations were observed for the LiSN-S High Cue, LiSN-S Low Cue, RAVLT total, and TMT B tests. No significant correlations were observed between exposure proxies (years of participation and self-reported number of concussions) and any speech-in-noise measures and cognitive measures. These exploratory findings, while not establishing causality or clinical impairment, warrant further investigation into speech-in-noise performance as a potential and previously under-considered area of vulnerability in contact sport athletes exposed to repetitive head impacts (RHI).

title: Rare non-coding variant rs890306703 is genetically associated with early-onset severe retinal degeneration.

Polyphenol-starch complex regulates the butyric acid-NXPH4-PDX1 pathway and alters pancreatic α- and β-cell marker expression profiles via the gut microbiota to stabilize postprandial blood glucose levels in mice with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Postprandial hyperglycemia is a major driver of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), yet whether food-derived starch-polyphenol complexes improve glycemic control through gut microbiota-dependent changes in pancreatic islet cell marker expression profiles remains unclear. Here, we show that a high-hydrostatic-pressure-treated complex of Lonicera caerulea berry polyphenols and wheat starch (LCBP-WS) forms resistant starch with an A + V crystalline structure and ameliorates postprandial hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in male T2DM mice. LCBP-WS increased intestinal butyrate and GLP-1 levels, reduced glucagon, improved glucose tolerance and pancreatic pathology, and altered pancreatic α-to-β-cell marker expression profiles, accompanied by increased INS, NKX6.1, NXPH4 and PDX1 expression. Antibiotic depletion of the gut microbiota largely abolished these benefits, increasing the glucose excursion area under the curve by 52.8% and suppressing the H3K27ac-NXPH4-PDX1 axis. In αTC1.6 cells, butyrate reversed high-glucose-induced endocrine dysfunction and induced changes in α-and βcell marker expression profiles. Mechanistically, butyrate enhanced H3K27ac enrichment at the NXPH4 locus, upregulated NXPH4 transcription, and stabilized PDX1 by limiting its proteasomal degradation. Genetic silencing of NXPH4 attenuated the effects of butyrate, whereas PDX1 overexpression partially restored them. Together, these suggest identify a gut microbiota-butyrate-H3K27ac-NXPH4-PDX1 pathway linking a food-derived resistant starch complex to changes in pancreatic islet cell marker expression and glycemic control, and suggest starch-polyphenol complexes as a potential dietary strategy for T2DM.

title: Raw material grade-associated differences in Ancha tea infusion quality revealed by sensory-instrumental evaluation, metabolomics and integrative multivariate analysis.
abstract: Raw material grade is associated with the quality of processed tea, yet how multicomponent metabolic variation relates to taste and infusion color differences among Te Gong (TG), Gong Jian (GJ) and Mao Jian (MJ) Ancha teas remains unclear. This study combined sensory evaluation, instrumental taste and color measurements, and targeted and untargeted metabolomics with exploratory multivariate integration to characterize these relationships. TG received the highest sensory taste and infusion color scores, whereas MJ showed a higher electronic tongue sweetness response despite its lower sensory taste score. Chemical profiling revealed a gallated catechin- and caffeine-rich profile in TG, higher epicatechin and epigallocatechin contents in MJ, and relatively high gallocatechin gallate and gallic acid contents in GJ, indicating distinct compositional patterns rather than a uniform grade-dependent concentration gradient. Exploratory weighted correlation network analysis identified 114 grade-associated metabolites, dominated by phenylpropanoids and polyketides, particularly flavonoids; detected free amino acids were enriched toward TG, whereas d-glucose and sucrose were enriched toward MJ. Block partial least squares integration linked the TG-associated quality responses with gallated catechins, caffeine and taste-related amino acids, and the MJ-associated sweetness response with sugars, while revealing overlapping but non-identical metabolite associations with taste and infusion color. Together, these findings provide an association-based chemical framework for interpreting Ancha tea grade differentiation, extending quality characterization from individual constituents and attributes to multicomponent metabolic patterns linked to multidimensional infusion quality.

title: Curdione alleviates DSS-induced colitis by inhibiting of M1-like macrophage in mice.
abstract: Curdione (Cur) has been showed as an effective natural ingredient to possess anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer properties. However, its therapeutic effects in colitis remain under-explored. We hypothesized that Cur would alleviate dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis via inhibiting M1-like macrophage. The effect of Cur on mice macrophage was evaluated using flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and macrophage depletion treatment. Cur reduced colonic and serum pro-inflammatory cytokines and macrophage infiltration in mice during DSS challenge. But such protection could not be recapitulated with macrophage depletion in mice suggesting macrophages are essential for the therapeutic efficacy of Cur in colitis. Mechanistically, Cur restored gut tryptophan metabolic network, enriching Indole-3-ethanol (I3E), 5-Hydroxyindole-3-acetic acid (5-HIAA) and Kynurenic acid (KYNA), which significantly reduced Toll-like receptor 2 (Tlr2) and M1 macrophage marker CD86 expression in colitis mice. Collectively, Cur treatment ameliorated DSS-induced colitis by partially inhibition M1 macrophage polarization, which might be associated with an regulation of tryptophan metabolism and downregulation of Tlr2 expression.

title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Sleep: Integrating Multichannel Signals for Comprehensive Assessment.
abstract: Sleep medicine generates rich, multimodal physiologic data that has traditionally been reduced to summary metrics through labor-intensive manual interpretation. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is transforming the field by enabling scalable, reproducible, and integrated analysis of polysomnographic signals. This review examines 5 interrelated frontiers of multimodal AI in sleep medicine: foundation models pre-trained on diverse biosignal datasets that may unify analysis across devices and populations; automated sleep staging systems that match individual expert reliability; AI-driven respiratory analysis that moves beyond the Apnea-Hypopnea Index toward continuous, endotype-level characterization of sleep-disordered breathing; AI-derived sleep biomarkers, including electroencephalography microstructure, brain age.

title: Sleep and Neurodegeneration: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Early Detection and Personalized Care.
abstract: Sleep disturbances are increasingly recognized as both risk factors for and prodromal markers of neurodegenerative diseases. The glymphatic system provides a mechanistic basis for the bidirectional relationship between disrupted sleep and misfolded protein accumulation. Artificial intelligence (AI) applications, including automated sleep staging, wearable monitoring, and digital treatments, offer scalable tools for early detection and personalized sleep health promotion. This review examines current evidence linking sleep medicine, neurodegeneration, and AI.

title: Pediatric Sleep Medicine: Tailoring Artificial Intelligence Solutions for the Youngest Patients.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly relevant to pediatric sleep medicine, a field defined by complex physiologic signals, longitudinal behavioral data, time-intensive expert scoring, and uneven access to subspecialty care. Because sleep physiology, respiratory control, symptom expression, and monitoring tolerance change across development, pediatric practice cannot rely on adult-derived algorithms without age-specific training and validation. This review highlights the current evidence for AI-assisted obstructive sleep apnea screening and severity estimation, automated sleep staging, and more informative analysis of actigraphy and wearable signals. These tools may help reduce burden, support home and longitudinal monitoring, and streamline human review.

title: Artificial Intelligence Applied to Nocturnal and Daytime Neurophysiology and Actigraphy in Central Disorders of Hypersomnolence.
abstract: Central disorders of hypersomnolence including narcolepsy type 1 and 2 (NT1 and NT2) and idiopathic hypersomnia (IH), are characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and assessed using complex multimodal data (polysomnography, multiple sleep latency test, actigraphy, biomarkers). These features make hypersomnolence disorders well suited for machine learning approaches. Recent advances show high diagnostic performance for NT1, but lower accuracy for NT2 and IH due to heterogeneity and lack of biomarkers. Unsupervised methods challenge current classifications. This review summarizes artificial intelligence applications, highlights key limitations (small datasets, diagnostic instability), and outlines future directions, emphasizing multimodal, longitudinal, and self-supervised approaches toward data-driven phenotyping.

title: Digital endpoints as outcome measures in orthopaedic care and their psychometric properties: a scoping review protocol.
Long-Read Sequencing Resolves Phase in Prenatal Congenital Chloride Diarrhea Resulting From Inherited and de novo SLC26A3 Variants.
Physiological Arousal During Alcohol Cue Exposure in Adult Drinkers: Sex Differences in Neural and Clinical Correlates: Alcohol Cue Exposure and Arousal.
abstract: Cue exposure contributes to craving and reinforces alcohol misuse, potentially by altering interoceptive processing and physiological arousal. However, few studies have reported changes in physiological arousal or their neural underpinnings in response to alcohol cues. Here, we addressed these questions in 94 adult drinkers (39 females; age mean ± SD: 59.1 ± 19.1 years and range: 19-85 years) who underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging and skin conductance recording during alcohol and neutral cue exposures and completed clinical assessments including the Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT; mean ± SD: 4.4 ± 5.5). Imaging data were processed with published routines and evaluated at a corrected threshold. The results showed significantly higher skin conductance response in 'alcohol>neutral' blocks (SCRAl-Ne) in females than in males. However, SCRAl-Ne was positively correlated with participants' AUDIT scores in males but not in females. SCRAl-Ne was also positively correlated with global positive alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking scores in males but not in females. A voxel-wise two sample test of the contrast 'alcohol>neutral' did not show any clusters with significant sex differences in cue reactivity. Whole-brain regression of the same contrast on AUDIT scores identified a large cluster in the perigenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC), with the beta estimates showing a significant positive correlation with the SCRAl-Ne, again in males only. These sex differences were all confirmed by slope tests. Thus, males with more drinking problems showed higher arousal as well as the pgACC response to alcohol cues in association with alcohol expectancy and novelty seeking. In chain mediation modelling, the pgACC response and alcohol expectancy interlinked SCRAl-Ne and AUDIT scores in males. In contrast, we failed to observe any significant neural or psychological correlates of physiological arousal, despite higher SCRAl-Ne, in females. With the caveat of a smaller sample size for females, these findings highlight sex and individual differences in physiological responses to alcohol cues and the neural and psychological underpinnings in male adult drinkers. Whether or how physiological arousal may play a role in the pathophysiology of alcohol misuse remains to be investigated for females.

title: Hospital-wide massive transfusion over time: Indications, treatment strategies, and clinical outcomes.
abstract: Massive transfusion (MT) is a lifesaving intervention for severe hemorrhage. Contemporary data on indications, transfusion practices, and outcomes across a broad in-hospital population remain limited. This retrospective cohort study included adult patients receiving MT at Karolinska University Hospital between 2016 and 2021. MT was defined as transfusion of ≥10 red blood cell (RBC) units within 24 h. Data were obtained from the hospital transfusion registry and medical records. A total of 486 MT events were identified. Median age was 60 years (interquartile range [IQR] 46-70), and 65.6% of patients were male. The most common indications were trauma (15.6%), abdominal cancer surgery (15.0%), cardiothoracic surgery (14.0%), and vascular surgery (12.3%). The overall median RBC:plasma:platelet ratio was 5:5:1, consistent with balanced transfusion strategies. MT was more frequently associated with acute than elective procedures (67.2% vs. 32.8%, p < 0.001). Fibrinogen, tranexamic acid, and prothrombin complex concentrate were administered in 69.5%, 52.1%, and 13.6% of cases, respectively. Mortality was 10.3% at 24 h and 31.7% at 30 days. The annual number of MT events decreased significantly during the study period (p < 0.001), corresponding to an approximately 40% reduction between 2016 and 2021. MT was required across a wide range of surgical and medical specialties and remained associated with substantial mortality. Balanced transfusion strategies were well implemented, whereas the use of adjunct hemostatic therapies varied considerably. The marked reduction in MT events over time suggests improvements in hemorrhage management and bleeding control.

title: Discovery, optimization, and Phase 1 evaluation of a novel, orally available GLP-1R/GIPR dual agonist.
abstract: The efficacy and convenience of anti-diabetic and anti-obesity therapeutics have surged in recent years due to the emergence of incretin-based poly-pharmacological approaches as well as advances in the oral delivery of peptide drugs. We sought to combine both strategies in an orally deliverable dual agonist of the GLP-1 and GIP receptors. We designed a panel of unimolecular, fatty-acylated peptide dual agonists, which was screened for receptor potencies in cell-based assay systems. NNC0130 was selected to advance into clinical studies using both oral and subcutaneous administration. NNC0130 exhibited in vitro potency comparable to semaglutide at human GLP-1R and to tirzepatide at human GIPR, with a chemical structure compatible with semi-recombinant production. Its human half-life of 76-89 hours was deemed suitable for once-daily oral administration. In a multiple-ascending dose trial in participants with overweight or obesity and with separate subcutaneous and oral cohorts, daily subcutaneous administration of NNC0130 escalating from 0.3 to 3.0 mg per dose provided a placebo-corrected mean body weight loss of 9% after 12 weeks of treatment and 12% after 15 weeks. Daily oral administration escalating from 5 to 50 mg per dose provided a placebo-corrected mean body weight loss of 4% after 12 weeks, which was not statistically significantly different from zero. The relative oral bioavailability when co-formulated with permeation enhancer salcaprozate sodium was estimated to 1.6-2.2% versus s.c. administration. The modest weight lowering efficacy of orally administered NNC0130 highlights the continued challenges of low oral bioavailability of acylated peptides. However, the substantial efficacy observed with subcutaneous administration motivated advancement into Phase 2 clinical development.

title: Quality and Quantity of Research Publications by Iranian Neurosurgeons: A Scopus-Based Bibliometric Analysis of the 21st Century.
abstract: Bibliometric analyses can clarify research productivity, collaboration, and evidence quality. Given expanding neuroscience research, improved bibliographic indexing, and the growth of neurosurgical practice in Iran, a comprehensive evaluation of Iranian neurosurgeons' publications is warranted to characterize long-term trends and guide future national research priorities. Iranian neurosurgeons were identified through a list obtained from the Iranian Medical Council Organization. These surgeons were verified, and their publications published through December 31, 2024, were identified through Scopus, followed by deduplication. Extracted variables included author characteristics, authorship roles, collaboration patterns, journal metrics, study design, citation counts, research topics, and levels of evidence (LOE). LOEs were classified from I (highest) to V (lowest) using an adapted Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) 2009 framework, and temporal trends were analyzed across three time periods (2000-2010, 2011-2020, and 2021-2024). Overall, 4,338 unique publications were included. Publication output increased over time: 617 studies (2000-2010), 2,206 (2011-2020), and 1,515 (2021-2024). Tehran accounted for 58% of publications, followed by Fars, East Azerbaijan, and Razavi Khorasan. International co-authorship increased from 119 (19%) in 2000-2010 to 513 (34%) in 2021-2024 (p < 0.001). The median journal impact factor (IF) rose from 1.7 to 2.0. Most studies were level IV (40%) and level V (23%) of evidence. Among trauma-related studies, 45% were classified as Level I-II. Iranian neurosurgeons' contributions to academic publications increased during the 21st century, accompanied by growing international collaboration. High-level clinical evidence was limited, highlighting the need for strengthened research infrastructure and methodological support.

title: MMP-9 and MMP-2 Contribute to Arsenic-Induced Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption Through Tight Junction Protein Loss in Cerebral Microvascular Endothelial Cells.
journal: Food and chemical toxicology : an international journal published for the British Industrial Biological Research Association
abstract: Chronic drinking-water arsenic exposure threatens neurological health, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction contributes to arsenic neurotoxicity. Although arsenic reduces tight junction proteins (TJPs), including ZO-1, Occludin and Claudin-5, the mechanisms underlying TJP loss remain unclear. We used C57BL/6N mice exposed to sodium arsenite for 12 weeks and mouse brain microvascular endothelial bEnd.3 cells to investigate whether matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) and MMP-2 are involved in linking arsenic exposure to endothelial barrier injury. In vivo, arsenic exposure dose-dependently increased BBB permeability, disrupted endothelial tight junction ultrastructure, reduced endothelial TJP signals, and increased MMP-9 and MMP-2 abundance in cerebral microvessels, with altered spatial localization of these proteins. In vitro, sodium arsenite dose-dependently reduced TJP expression while increasing MMP-9 and MMP-2 expression and MMP enzymatic activity. The MMP-2/MMP-9 inhibitor SB-3CT suppressed MMP enzymatic activity and partially restored arsenic-induced TJP loss; the selective MMP-9 inhibitor JNJ0966 and MMP-2 siRNA knockdown each partially alleviated arsenic-induced TJP depletion, supporting the involvement of both proteases in this process. Collectively, our findings suggest that MMP-9 and MMP-2 contribute to arsenic-induced endothelial TJP loss, potentially contributing to BBB dysfunction. These findings provide insight into arsenic neurotoxicity and identify potential molecular targets for intervention.

title: An unfair fight: multiorgan mechanisms that disarm host defenses and deplete the physiological reserve needed to withstand infection and sepsis after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes vulnerability to infection and sepsis that cannot be explained by impaired mobility and healthcare-related exposure alone. SCI is known to disrupt multiple organ systems, but how these disruptions collectively shift the balance between host protection and microbial challenge remains poorly defined. In this narrative review, we examine how systemic dysfunction caused by SCI impairs the capacity to prevent infection, contain established pathogens, and withstand escalating infectious stress. We organize clinical and experimental evidence around functions that together determine host protection: barrier protection, immune surveillance, pathogen clearance, and physiological reserve. The first three restrict microbial access, establishment, and burden, whereas physiological reserve determines the capacity of tissues and organs to maintain function as infectious stress escalates. We distinguish experimentally demonstrated mechanisms from clinical associations for infection vulnerability and examine how injury level and time shape these vulnerabilities. We trace how pneumonia, urinary tract infection, and pressure wound infection can progress to sepsis, and delineate the mechanisms that create increasingly unequal contests in which pathogens encounter a host with progressively weakened defenses, depleted physiological reserve, and an environment that favors pathogen establishment and persistence. This framework identifies testable gaps and a translational path toward earlier risk stratification, management of infection within the context of SCI, and potential strategies to preserve or restore host defense and resilience to infection, shifting the balance of this unequal contest back toward the host.

title: FGFR1-driven brachyury promotes endothelial-like differentiation of glioblastoma stem cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling pathways.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intensive vascular proliferation that is essential for tumor growth. Recent studies indicate the existence of tumor-derived endothelial-like cells can arise from the differentiation of GBM stem cells (GSCs). The transcription factor brachyury plays a critical role in promoting stem cell identity and vasculogenesis during normal embryonic development. However, its involvement in endothelial-like differentiation of GSCs remains unknown. By integrating clinical bioinformatics from GBM databases with preclinical in vitro and in vivo models, including patient-derived GSC cell lines and xenografts, we found that brachyury is highly expressed in GBM tissues and correlates with angiogenesis genes. Our study demonstrated that brachyury is activated by fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), which subsequently promotes GSC differentiation into endothelial-like cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling. GSCs with high brachyury expression display great sensitivity to selective FGFR inhibitors in vascular tube formation assays. In vivo pharmacological targeting of FGFR1 with inhibitor E7090 or brachyury gene editing using Cas9/gRNA suppresses GBM neovascularization and tumor growth. Furthermore, gene signature analysis of GBM patients further demonstrated that a lower FGFR1/brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signature score significantly correlates with favorable overall survival outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of FGFR1-driven brachyury activation in GSC-derived neovascularization and suggest that targeting the FGFR1-directed brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling represents a promising therapeutic strategy for GBM.

title: Training Interbrain Synchrony through Dyadic Neurofeedback Modulates Empathy-for-Pain.
abstract: Dyadic neurofeedback offers a socially grounded approach for modulating neural processes that unfold between interacting individuals. While recent work demonstrates that dyadic neurofeedback can enhance inter-brain synchrony during interaction, whether its effects extend beyond the trained dyad remains unclear. Here, we examined whether dyadic neurofeedback targeting inter-brain synchrony in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) is associated with changes in empathy-for-pain toward unfamiliar social targets. One hundred and eighty-six participants, randomly assigned to dyads, completed three neurofeedback training sessions within one week. Feedback was contingent on real-time IFG inter-brain synchrony in the neurofeedback group or on prerecorded signals in the sham-feedback control group. Empathy-for-pain was assessed before and after training. IFG inter-brain synchrony increased significantly across sessions in the neurofeedback group but not in the control group. Empathy-for-pain ratings showed different trajectories across conditions in the primary raw-data analysis, decreasing significantly in the sham-feedback group while remaining relatively stable in the neurofeedback group. A secondary analysis adjusting for a previously observed task-specific test-retest decline showed a significant increase in the neurofeedback group. Individuals with lower baseline trait empathy showed larger training-related increases in IFG inter-brain synchrony. Network analyses suggested broader changes involving IFG-IPL connectivity.
