Structural equation modeling further identified significant associations among training-related intra-brain synchrony, inter-brain synchrony, and empathy-for-pain change, consistent with the proposed relationship among these processes. Together, the findings indicate that dyadic neurofeedback can modulate IFG inter-brain synchrony across repeated training and may influence the trajectory of empathy-for-pain responding beyond the immediate training partner.

title: Desync and connect: Noninvasive MEG evidence of long-range coupling between locally desynchronized regions.
abstract: A prevailing assumption in systems neuroscience is that long-range phase coupling between cortical regions requires locally synchronized oscillatory activity within each interacting area. Here we ask whether distal phase coupling can be detected from MEG data when both interacting regions undergo concurrent event-related desynchronization (ERD). Using controlled simulations with progressively disrupted local phase coherence, we first establish that the Context-Dependent PSIICOS (CD-PSIICOS) framework - a projection-based connectivity estimator that separates power-dominated spatial leakage from interaction-specific cross-spectral structure - can recover distal coupling under increasing local phase dispersion, whereas estimators based on the imaginary part of the cross-spectrum fail at near-zero lags. We then analyzed recordings of a center-out reaching dataset from nine participants. A group decomposition of the coupling time courses identifies four long-range networks in alpha (8-13 Hz) and two in beta (15-25 Hz), each with its own time window. For each network we follow the local connections between its own sources as the power-dominated subspace is projected out, separating leakage-driven from leakage-resistant local coupling. In the earliest alpha network the leakage-resistant pairs stay at or below their pre-stimulus level at every rank while the power of the same sources falls, so this interhemispheric interaction may have no stable local counterpart. In the beta networks such a counterpart does survive, but the coupling it carries is an order of magnitude weaker than the long-range coupling of the same sources. Only in the latest alpha window, by which time power has returned to baseline, do local and long-range coupling rise together. Factorising the coupling into the amplitude of the single-trial cross-terms and the consistency of their phases separates the same cases: in the networks without a local counterpart, phase consistency increases inside the window while the amplitude of the cross-terms declines, whereas in the network whose local coupling rises with it, the increase reflects a growth of the cross-terms themselves rather than any improvement in their phase agreement. Long-range phase coupling can therefore persist, and in places strengthen, between regions undergoing macroscopic ERD, and noninvasive MEG can resolve this dissociation when leakage-aware estimation is employed.

title: Clip-to-trial: EEG-based decoding network with long short-term self-attention for DRDS recognition.
abstract: Dynamic random-dot stereograms (DRDS) elicit stereoscopic perception associated with high-level binocular visual processing, which can be decoded from EEG signals. However, existing EEG-based approaches predominantly rely on clip-level learning, leading to feature-label misalignment and limited modeling of trial-level spatiotemporal dependencies. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a clip-to-trial long short-term self-attention network (C2T-LSTSA) for EEG-based DRDS recognition. The proposed method first extracts discriminative spatiotemporal features from EEG clips using a multi-scale local feature extraction module. A trial-level feature reconstruction module is then introduced to explicitly map clip-level representations into semantically consistent trial-level features. Furthermore, a long short-term self-attention module is employed to jointly model local temporal dependencies within each reconstructed trial representation and global dependencies among multiple reconstructed trial representations derived from the same original EEG trial. Extensive experiments on three EEG datasets collected from strabismus patients demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches under both subject-dependent and subject-independent evaluation protocols, indicating its effectiveness and robustness for objective assessment of stereoscopic visual function. The reference datasets are available at https://github.com/YANGeeg/TJU-SRD-datasets and the code is at https://github.com/wu860898-design/C2T-LSTSA.

title: Behavioral and neurobiological effects of vicarious social defeat stress in rodents: a scoping review.
abstract: Psychosocial stress is a risk factor for psychiatric disorders, and evidence indicates that witnessing adversity can be harmful. Vicarious social defeat stress (VSDS) models the indirect psychosocial suffering that arises when a rodent perceives the social defeat of a conspecific without being physically attacked. Despite the methodologically heterogeneous growth of this evidence, a map of its effects on observer animals was lacking. This scoping review aimed to map the behavioral effects and neurobiological alterations reported in rodents exposed to VSDS, and to characterize paradigm variants, exposure parameters and moderating variables (sex, age, strain). Its contribution is a detailed, observer-focused integration of behavioral domains, biological substrates and protocol characteristics across 60 studies. It was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews; the protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework, and sources were searched without language or date restrictions. The most frequently reported phenotypes were social avoidance, anxiety-like behavior and anhedonia, accompanied in subsets of studies by depression-like behavior, cognitive deficits, altered fear learning and escalated substance intake. Most studies reported neurobiological measures, with a predominance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and adaptations across the mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic system, extended amygdala, hippocampal formation, medial prefrontal cortex and neuroimmune signatures. Direct witness-versus-defeated comparisons revealed qualitative convergence alongside dissociations, while females remained under-represented. VSDS yields consistently reported affective phenotypes and circuit-level adaptations, positioning it as a relevant model of indirect trauma whose advancement depends on methodological harmonization, sex-balanced designs and investigation of socially transmitted stress.

title: A superconserved orphan GPCR in brain function and disease: insights into GPR85.
abstract: G protein‑coupled receptor 85 (GPR85), also known as superconserved receptor expressed in brain 2 (SREB2), is a highly conserved orphan class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) with preferential expression in the central nervous system (CNS). Since its identification, GPR85 has emerged as a critical regulator of neuronal development, synaptic function, and circuit excitability, with accumulating evidence implicating its involvement in cognitive and behavioral processes. Moreover, further studies have linked dysregulation of GPR85 to neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), highlighting its potential relevance to human brain disease. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of GPR85 biology by integrating findings from animal models with emerging evidence from human studies as well as our analyses of publicly available human single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic datasets to refine current understanding of GPR85 organization in the human brain. Together, these perspectives support a revised view of GPR85 as a context-dependent modulator of brain function operating across multiple cellular systems, highlighting the need to determine its roles in brain physiology, pathology, and therapeutic targeting.

title: Efficacy of ORM-12741 on agitation/aggression symptoms in participants with Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: ORM-12741 is a potent and selective alpha-2C adrenoceptor antagonist. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of ORM-12741 in treating agitation/aggression symptoms in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD). This was a phase II, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 308 community-dwelling participants with mild to moderate AD (Mini-Mental State Examination [MMSE] scores 10 to 24) and Neuropsychiatric Inventory agitation/aggression scores of ≥4. Participants were randomized to 60 or 120 mg of ORM-12741 or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks. Efficacy was assessed primarily with the sum of Neuropsychiatric Inventory Clinician Rating (NPI-C) Agitation and Aggression domain scores. In addition, effects on cognition, psychotic, depressive, and overall neuropsychiatric symptoms were assessed. No relevant treatment effects as compared to placebo group were detected on either the primary or secondary efficacy measures. ORM-12741 was generally well tolerated. The study does not support the efficacy of ORM-12741 on agitation/aggression symptoms in patients with AD.

title: Decomposed arterial stiffness and NfL-cognition association in older adults: The IGNITE study.
abstract: Neurofilament light chain (NfL) indexes neuroaxonal injury and relates to poorer cognition. Higher carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV) arterial stiffness strengthens NfL-cognition associations, but reflects both pressure-standardized structural stiffness (S-PWV) and transient hemodynamic load-dependent pulse wave velocity (LD-PWV). We tested which component drives this interaction. Plasma NfL and cfPWV were measured in 552 cognitively unimpaired older adults. cfPWV was decomposed into S-PWV and LD-PWV. Five latent cognitive domains were modeled. Linear regression tested PWV moderators of NfL-cognition associations. NfL correlated with all domains (r = -0.116 to -0.185; P 0.09). Nominal interactions were more consistent for S-PWV. Findings did not provide multiplicity-adjusted evidence of component-specific moderation.ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02875301.

title: Multi-platform comparison of plasma phosphorylated tau assays: analytical and workflow factors drive clinical implementation decisions.
abstract: Multiple plasma phosphorylated tau assays are now commercially available for Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet clinical laboratories lack comprehensive comparative data to guide implementation. We assessed diagnostic accuracy and analytical performance in 273 participants with paired plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). CSF AD core biomarkers served as the reference standard. Index tests included three plasma tau phosphorylated at residue 217 (pTau217) assays (Roche, Fujirebio, Meso Scale Discovery [MSD]) and a pTau181 assay (Roche). Participants: median age 70 [IQR: 64 to 76] years, 42% female, and 60% AD-positive. pTau217 assays showed comparable accuracy (area under the curve [AUC] 0.88 to 0.89) exceeding pTau181 (AUC 0.85). All assays were resistant to hemolysis, icterus, and lipemia. Automated assays (Roche, Fujirebio) showed superior analytical precision and freeze/thaw stability (≥6 cycles) compared to the manual MSD assay (two cycles). With comparable diagnostic accuracy across pTau217 platforms, analytical performance, and operational suitability became decisive implementation differentiators.

title: Excessive censoring degrades individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized TMS targets.
abstract: Head motion systematically biases functional connectivity (FC) estimates in resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). A common mitigation strategy is to censor high-motion volumes and discard high-motion runs. However, overly stringent censoring risks discarding signal alongside noise, potentially degrading FC estimates. Here, we test the efficacy of various censoring strategies on individual-specific cortical parcellations and personalized transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) target selection. Using precision-fMRI datasets comprising 50 individuals, we define individualized "ground-truth" references from ≥1 hour of low-motion data per participant. We then simulate 10-minute or 20-minute rs-fMRI sessions with varying motion levels from the remaining data, yielding final samples of 22 and 19 participants, respectively. Higher motion produces parcellations and TMS targets that deviate further from the ground-truth references. However, at any given motion level, lenient censoring produces higher quality parcellations and personalized TMS targets than strict censoring. The improvement is comparable to doubling scan duration from 20 to 40 minutes under strict censoring. With personalized connectome-guided TMS, a common dilemma is whether to re-scan patients with only high-motion runs. A mixed-motion session with one low-motion run and one high-motion run may often be considered usable after discarding the high-motion run and strict censoring. We find that lenient censoring of high-motion-only sessions yields TMS targets comparable to-or even better than-those derived from strictly censored mixed-motion sessions. Therefore, within the motion range and parcellation/TMS targeting frameworks evaluated here, patients may not need to be re-scanned solely because all runs exceed strict censoring criteria.

title: Three-Dimensional Gait Analysis in STXBP1-Related Disorder.
abstract: STXBP1-related disorder (STXBP1-RD), caused by pathogenic variants in the STXBP1 gene, is a rare neurodevelopmental condition, characterized by early-onset seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability (ID), and prominent motor dysfunction. Despite the high prevalence of motor symptoms, systematic gait characterization remains limited. The aim of this study was therefore to quantitatively assess gait in participants with STXBP1-RD. In this cross-sectional study, we included ambulatory participants aged 6 years or older with genetically confirmed STXBP1-RD. Instrumented 3D gait analysis (i3DGA) was performed to objectively quantify gait. Functional mobility was assessed with the Functional Mobility Scale (FMS) and Mobility Questionnaire 28 (MobQues28). Caregiver health-related quality of life was evaluated using the PedsQL-Family Impact Module (PedsQL-FIM). We explored associations between gait, functional mobility, STXBP1-variant type, and clinical features (ID, age at seizure onset, seizure frequency, and age at onset of independent walking). Correspondence between i3DGA and the Edinburgh Visual Gait Score (EVGS), an observational gait assessment, was investigated. Nineteen participants were included. Compared with typically developing peers, participants with STXBP1-RD had significantly reduced walking speed, step length, and stride length. Gait patterns were highly variable, with the most frequent pattern being an externally rotated foot progression angle (FPA), present in 15 of 19 participants. At home, 94.12% of the participants (16/17) walked independently, yet community mobility was more variable: 70.59% (12/17) walked independently, 11.76% (2/17) with aid, and 17.65% (3/17) used a wheelchair, indicating increasing limitations with distance and environmental complexity. Earlier acquisition of independent walking strongly predicted later unassisted ambulation at the community level (p < 0.001). The median MobQues28 score was 57.14% and median PedsQL-FIM score was 60.42%, indicating a moderate level of mobility limitations and reduced health-related quality of life of caregivers. EVGS was highly positive correlated with i3DGA (p = 0.001). Quantitative gait analysis in participants with STXBP1-RD demonstrates heterogenous kinematic deviations, with an externally rotated FPA emerging as the most common pattern. Age at independent walking was a clinically relevant predictor of later functional mobility. EVGS showed strong correspondence with i3DGA and may offer a more practical, semiquantitative assessment for broader use. These findings inform clinical decision making and guide the selection of scalable outcome measures for natural history studies and interventional trials.

title: Cognitive and brain reserve in bilingual speakers with clinical AD variants.
abstract: Bilingualism may confer resilience through enhanced neural integrity. However, evidence for its neuroprotective effect is mixed, and studies across Alzheimer's disease (AD) variants are limited. This study examined gray matter volume (GMV) differences between bilinguals and monolinguals with amnestic AD and logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (lvPPA). In 125 amnestic AD and 78 lvPPA participants with neuropsychological assessments and structural magnetic resonance imaging, we analyzed GMV differences between monolinguals and bilinguals within each variant, adjusting for demographic covariates. In amnestic AD, bilinguals showed lower GMV than monolinguals in several regions, including bilateral fusiform and right occipital regions, after correction for multiple comparisons. In lvPPA, regional differences did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, although at the nominal threshold, bilinguals showed lower GMV in temporal and occipital regions and greater GMV in inferior parietal regions. Cognitive performance was comparable between monolinguals and bilinguals within each group. Comparable cognitive performance despite lower GMV is consistent with a potential role of bilingualism in cognitive reserve. The observed regional patterns in lvPPA are exploratory and require replication in a larger sample.

title: Intranasal nano-immunotherapy for glioma: bypassing the blood-brain barrier, reprogramming the immune microenvironment, and bridging preclinical validation.
abstract: Glioma, particularly glioblastoma, remains difficult to treat because of limited drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, profound immune suppression, and insufficient intracranial exposure of systemic immunotherapies. Intranasal nano-immunotherapy is being explored as a potential strategy that may integrate noninvasive nose-to-brain delivery with nanocarrier-mediated immune reprogramming. Intranasal administration may partially bypass conventional vascular barriers through olfactory, trigeminal, mucosal, cerebrospinal-fluid, and perivascular transport routes, while nanoparticles are designed to protect immune-active payloads, support brain tumor targeting, and enable controlled release. Current evidence spans three distinct levels: direct intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy, intranasal glioma nanodelivery without demonstrated immune reprogramming, and non-intranasal glioma nano-immunotherapy that provides mechanistic support for future intranasal adaptation. Across these evidence levels, investigated platforms include peptide-guided nanomicelles, lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic nanoparticles, ferritin-based nanovectors, spherical nucleic acids, extracellular vesicles, bacterial outer membrane vesicles, and stimuli-responsive systems. These platforms can deliver immune-activating cargos, such as STING or TLR agonists; gene-regulatory cargos, such as siRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 components; and microenvironment-modulating cargos, such as chemokine-axis inhibitors, checkpoint-modulating agents, and combination payloads. Through these payloads, intranasal nanoplatforms may activate innate immune sensing, reverse myeloid-mediated suppression, enhance T-cell infiltration, and induce immunogenic cell death. However, translation remains limited by dosing uncertainty, species differences in nasal anatomy, mucosal and neurological safety concerns, manufacturing complexity, and incomplete immune pharmacodynamic validation. This review summarizes recent advances in intranasal and brain-targeted glioma nano-immunotherapy, highlights key immune mechanisms, and proposes a preclinical validation framework for evaluating whether experimental efficacy can be advanced toward clinically testable treatment designs.

title: Adult-Onset Limb-Girdle Phenotype Associated With a Homozygous PYROXD1 Variant: The Case of a North African Family.
abstract: Mutations in the pyridine nucleotide-disulfide oxide reductase domain-containing protein 1 (PYROXD1) gene are characteristically linked to early-onset congenital myofibrillar myopathy, typically presenting with generalized weakness, hypotonia, and respiratory insufficiency in infancy or early childhood. However, emerging evidence suggests phenotypic heterogeneity. We report the case of a 45-year-old Tunisian woman, born to non-consanguineous parents, who presented with a slowly progressive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) phenotype; her older brother, subsequently confirmed to carry the same homozygous variant, had a similar but more severe clinical history of proximal weakness. The patient's symptoms began at age 17 with running difficulties, progressing by age 35 to difficulty rising from a seated position and climbing stairs, and by age 45 to exertional dyspnea, dysphagia, and sleep-disordered breathing. Physical examination revealed a high-arched palate, scoliosis, joint hypermobility, limited ankle dorsiflexion, palatal weakness, and mild neck flexion weakness alongside a proximal-dominant limb-girdle pattern of weakness. Her brother showed a matching but more severe phenotype starting at age 12. Electrodiagnostic studies demonstrated normal nerve conduction and a non-irritable myopathy; serum creatine kinase was entirely normal, and pulmonary function testing revealed a restrictive ventilatory defect with mild obstructive sleep apnea on polysomnography. Clinical exome sequencing confirmed a pathogenic homozygous c.464A>G (p.Asn155Ser) mutation in the PYROXD1 gene in both affected siblings, with both parents confirmed as unaffected heterozygous carriers. This represents the first molecularly confirmed family with PYROXD1-related myopathy in Tunisia and North Africa, and only the second family identified across the African continent; a single unrelated Tunisian case harboring the same variant has also recently been reported. This case expands the known clinical spectrum of PYROXD1 variants to include adult-onset LGMD-like presentations with respiratory and bulbar involvement, emphasizes the diagnostic utility of recognizing associated dysmorphic features (scoliosis, high-arched palate, nasal speech, and joint hypermobility), and highlights the pivotal role of comprehensive genomic testing in atypical adult myopathies.

title: Atrial fibrillation phenotypes derived from multimodal data exhibit distinct electrophysiological substrate characteristics, symptom trajectories, and ablation outcomes.
abstract: The heterogeneity in response to catheter ablation amongst atrial fibrillation (AF) patients classified according to arrhythmia duration highlights the need for improved phenotyping. Multimodal assessment may better characterize the spectrum of pathophysiology present amongst patients classified as having paroxysmal or persistent AF. This study aimed to perform comprehensive multimodal pre-ablation phenotyping in patients undergoing AF ablation and evaluate associations with post-ablation arrhythmia recurrence, symptom burden, and bi-atrial substrate remodelling. In this multicentre prospective cohort study, 86 patients referred for first-time AF ablation (42% persistent AF) underwent pre-ablation phenotyping beyond usual care, incorporating patch-based ambulatory rhythm monitoring, atrial structural and functional MRI assessment, and formal symptom evaluation. Unsupervised K-means clustering was used to derive phenotypes. The primary outcome was 12-month arrhythmia recurrence; secondary analyses assessed symptom trajectories and bi-atrial substrate characteristics. Four AF phenotypes were identified. Arrhythmia recurrence occurred in 56.0%, 42.9%, 22.2%, and 19.0% of patients in Phenotypes 1-4, respectively (log-rank P = 0.032). Symptom trajectories differed across phenotypes, with the greatest improvements observed in Phenotypes 3 and 4. Exploratory electroanatomic mapping analyses demonstrated significant between-phenotype differences in bi-atrial bipolar voltage aligned with clinical trajectories. Importantly, phenotypes were not fully explained by conventional classification: Phenotype 2 experienced relatively high recurrence despite comprising predominantly paroxysmal AF patients whilst Phenotype 3 demonstrated favourable outcomes despite a high prevalence of persistent AF. Multimodal phenotyping identified distinct AF subgroups associated with differences in post-ablation recurrence, symptom trajectories, and electrophysiological substrate. This approach could improve pre-ablation risk stratification and shared decision-making. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05057507.

title: Mapping the technology-demand interface: how brain organoid evolution is reshaping the translational landscape of stroke.
journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
abstract: Stroke research faces a dual modeling barrier: interspecies divergence and oversimplified 2D cultures have contributed to the failure of many neuroprotective trials. Brain organoids, which provide human genetic backgrounds and 3D neural networks, offer a promising but incomplete solution. Existing reviews often address isolated technological aspects without linking them to stroke-specific demands. This narrative review establishes a "technological iteration-clinical demand" mapping matrix (Figure 1). We trace organoid evolution from static oxygen-glucose deprivation models to vascularized, assembloid, and microfluidic chip-integrated systems, and toward multi-organ coupling. We highlight how these advances may uncover human-specific neuroinflammation, proposed PANoptosis-like spatiotemporal cascades, and synaptic deficits mediated by human-specific genes such as SRGAP2C. We argue that the inability of animal models to resolve certain human-specific targets is driving organoids from static endpoint models toward dynamic platforms with perfusable vasculature and immune integration, although current systems remain at an early stage. We critically evaluate the preclinical role of organoids, defining scenarios where they may partially replace animal testing and where they cannot. Major bottlenecks include fetal-like organoid maturity (transcriptome approximately equivalent to gestational weeks 12-20) versus the average stroke onset age of about 70 years, and the absence of peripheral immune infiltration, which mediates a large fraction of secondary injury. We outline potential solutions including multi-omics integration, inducible aging, gene editing, and multi-organ chip coupling, and emphasize that standardized evaluation frameworks are needed to translate organoid findings into personalized stroke therapy.

title: Are cortical microcircuits optimized for information flux?-A simulation-based reverse engineering study.
abstract: A sufficiently large information flux in recurrent neural networks, quantified by the mutual information between successive network states, has been proposed as a marker of rich information-processing capabilities. This raises the question of whether biological neural networks, such as cortical microcircuits, may be structurally organized to enhance information flux. To investigate this possibility, we study a simplified model of the cortical layer 5 architecture, in which a densely and strongly interconnected core population is embedded within a larger supporting network. Surprisingly, we find that the embedding network exerts a pronounced flux-enhancing effect on the core dynamics. Systematic reverse-engineering analyses reveal that the embedding network primarily generates heterogeneous negative mean inputs that shift the core neurons into a higher-flux operating regime. Replacing the full time-dependent embedding signals by corresponding constant biases preserves this flux-enhancing effect, indicating that the detailed signal dynamics are not essential under the tested conditions. We further show that the information flux can be increased even beyond the biologically embedded case by applying optimized uniform or neuron-specific biases to the core neurons, and that similarly high values can emerge from a simple local adaptive-bias rule. Additional controls show that adaptive regulation and independently tuned inhibitory targeting further improve the embedded network, whereas removing the privileged strong-weight organization of the core abolishes the embedding advantage. These results suggest that the surrounding network acts as a distributed regulator that prevents a strongly recurrent core from becoming trapped in saturated, low-flux states, rather than as an optimizer of information flux. Our findings are relevant both for the functional interpretation of biological neural circuits and for the design of artificial recurrent systems such as reservoir computers.

title: Treatment of vascular dementia based on neuroprotection and neural repair strategies: from pathophysiology to natural products.
abstract: Vascular dementia (VaD) is a heterogeneous cognitive disorder associated with cerebrovascular pathology and persistent vascular dysfunction. Because effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited, natural products have attracted interest as potential interventions for the complex pathology of VaD. This review examines their effects from two complementary perspectives: neuroprotection and neural repair. Experimental studies indicate that natural products can influence several interconnected processes, including redox imbalance, neuroinflammation, cell survival, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, vascular remodeling, neurogenesis, and synaptic plasticity. However, the available evidence varies considerably among isolated compounds, botanical extracts, and herbal formulations. Some isolated compounds have been supported by relatively coherent relationships between molecular targets, tissue responses, and functional outcomes, whereas evidence from clinical studies remains much more limited. We therefore consider the current mechanistic evidence together with the major challenges in pharmacokinetics, quality control, and clinical translation.

title: Neuropsychiatric symptoms across the revised Alzheimer's disease clinical staging framework: A review of current evidence and implications.
abstract: The field of Alzheimer's disease (AD) research has seen major advances in understanding manifestations of AD-related neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS), including recent addition of NPS to the 2024 National Institute of Aging-Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) clinical staging framework. This focused review highlights key publications (49 in 2024; 28 in 2025) indexed in MEDLINE examining AD-related NPS, in alignment with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles guidelines. Data were thematically organized across NIA-AA clinical stages, with emphasis on measurement, diagnosis, and biomarker-cognition correlates of AD-related NPS. Together, these findings can inform future research and clinical practice through enhanced understanding of AD-related NPS and their relationships with pathology and clinical outcomes. Finally, three key priorities were identified for future research: (1) incorporating sex/gender and ethnocultural diversity; (2) integrating NPS assessment with cognitive, fluid, and neuroimaging biomarkers; and (3) including perspectives of individuals with lived experience to support personalized NPS management.

title: A network-control approach to seizure intervention via adjoint optimal control: a computational study on a connectome-coupled Hopf oscillator model.
abstract: Most existing open-loop Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) systems for drug-resistant epilepsy do not take into account the temporal dynamics of seizures or the spread of seizure activity. In this paper, we propose a closed-loop control system that models seizure prevention as a constraint on the nonlinear dynamics of the brain's structural network, and we evaluate it entirely in simulation. The structural network of the brain is modeled using the HCP-1065 (Human Connectome Project) connectome, which divides the brain into 360 regions. A densely connected sub-network of 60 brain regions was used to develop and test the proposed control system. Each region is modeled as a nonlinear supercritical Hopf oscillator, and the seizures modeled are focal-onset events that spread from a hippocampal onset zone through the connectome. A detector continuously monitors critical-slowing-down features of the dynamics, such as variance and lag-1 autocorrelation, to identify the approach to seizure activity. Two levels of control are applied: a linear-quadratic regulator (Level 1) that maintains the Hopf oscillators' basal state, and a dormant network-wide optimal controller (Level 2) that employs an adjoint-based optimal-control method (Adjoint Optimal Control; AOC) to provide pre-emptive control. Within the model, the predictive detector identifies the approach to the seizure transition with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.889 (95% confidence interval (CI) [0.820, 0.950]) on an independent test fold containing 50 trajectories per class, with a mean lead time of 56.9 model-time seconds; at the recall-maximizing operating point its false-positive rate is high (0.90 per 120-s seizure-free record), which we identify as the principal limitation of the present design. The controller prevented the seizure-like transition in 93% of 100 Monte Carlo simulations (95% CI: 86.2--96.6%) on the 60-node sub-network, against 21% for a connectome-naive targeting baseline; in the same continuously seizure-prone benchmark, a continuous open-loop push at matched amplitude and a PI controller suppressed every trial at lower energy, so the closed loop's advantages lie in pre-emptive lead time, network-wide homeostasis and delivering no stimulation when no risk is detected, not in energy per event. All validation uses synthetic trajectories generated by the same model; no patient or EEG data are used, and the results constitute a methodological proof-of-concept rather than evidence of clinical efficacy.

title: Health, Psychosocial Outcomes, and Help-seeking Behaviors Among Transgender Individuals in Urban India: A Mixed-methods Study.
abstract: Transgender individuals in India face elevated levels of health disparities rooted in social stigma, institutional discrimination, family rejection, and structural exclusion. The study aims to explore factors influencing health, psychosocial outcomes, and help-seeking behavior among transgender individuals in the Bangalore Urban Area. An analytical mixed-methods design, triangulating a quantitative cross-sectional assessment with qualitative thematic analysis. One hundred transgender individuals were recruited purposively via NGO networks and community settings. Instruments included the WHOQOL-BREF, the self-reporting questionnaire (SRQ-20), the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS), and the Transgender Identity Stigma Questionnaire (TISQ). Ten key stakeholders participated in semi-structured in-depth interviews. Statistical analyses comprised Spearman correlations, Kruskal-Wallis tests with Bonferroni post hoc corrections, and one-way ANOVA, with thematic analysis used for qualitative data. Moderate-to-high psychological distress was found in 35.4% of trans women and 33.3% of trans men. Felt normative stigma was higher than enacted stigma (Mean 24.79 vs. 13.58). Overall quality of life was moderate, with social relationships highest and physical health the lowest. Social support was significantly positively associated with all WHOQOL-BREF domains (r = 0.56, p < .01); mental distress negatively predicted all QoL domains. Family support significantly predicted psychological (H = 20.95, p < .001) and environmental QoL (H = 18.60, p < .001). Stigma, economic marginalization, and institutional mistrust collectively undermine mental health and quality of life. Peer networks and NGOs serve as primary protective and help-seeking conduits. Gender-affirming healthcare reforms, mandatory provider sensitization, and sustained community-led support are urgently needed.

title: Smartwatch-Derived Biomarkers Signal Pace of Biological Aging.
abstract: Biological aging varies substantially among individuals of the same chronological age, yet biological aging biomarkers require biospecimen collection and laboratory processing, limiting scalability for repeated monitoring. This study evaluated whether consumer smartwatch-derived digital biomarkers are associated with the pace of biological aging, quantified using DunedinPACE, a biomarker that measures biological aging rates. Baseline data were analyzed from the Healthy Minds for Life study within the Precision Aging Network. Among 1305 enrolled participants, 621 community-dwelling adults aged 50-79 years had both DunedinPACE and smartwatch data available. Smartwatch-derived biomarkers were grouped into mobility, cardiorespiratory physiology, sleep, and physiological stress domains. Associations with DunedinPACE were examined using Spearman correlations and adjusted linear regression models. Significant associations were observed across all four domains. Daily step count showed the strongest mobility-domain association with DunedinPACE (r = -0.25, p < 0.01). Mean sleep peripheral oxygen saturation showed the strongest sleep-domain association (r = -0.22, p < 0.01). Resting heart rate showed the strongest physiological stress-domain association (r = 0.24, p < 0.01). Adjusted regression models supported these findings, with lower daily mobility, poorer sleep oxygenation and efficiency, greater wake after sleep onset, and higher resting heart rate showing the most consistent associations with higher DunedinPACE values. Smartwatch-derived biomarkers captured a multidomain profile of accelerated biological aging characterized by lower mobility, poorer sleep health, and elevated physiological stress. Consumer wearables can provide low-burden, real-world indicators of biological vulnerability, although longitudinal studies are needed before clinical use.

title: Rehmannioside A alleviates oxidative stress and restores dopaminergic function via the PI3K/Akt pathway in a rotenone-induced Parkinson's disease model.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder; available treatments merely relieve symptoms, and no disease-modifying therapies are currently available. This study sought to explore the neuroprotective effects of Rehmannioside A (Re A) in rotenone-induced PD models and clarify its underlying mechanisms. A rotenone-induced PD rat model was established for in vivo experiments, with rats administered graded oral doses of Re A. Motor function was assessed via behavioral tests. Striatal oxidative stress markers and neurotransmitters were detected using biochemical assays and ELISA, respectively. HE staining was applied to observe histopathological alterations in the substantia nigra, and immunohistochemistry was used to visualize tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive neurons. Western blotting was performed to measure TH expression and key proteins of the PI3K/Akt pathway in brain tissue. For in vitro experiments, rotenone-challenged PC12 cells were treated with different concentrations of Re A. Cell viability was tested using CCK-8 assay, oxidative stress indicators were quantified, and protein levels were analyzed by Western blot. The PI3K inhibitor LY294002 was used to validate the reliance of protective effects on the PI3K/Akt pathway. In vivo, Re A significantly rescued weight loss and motor dysfunction, mitigated striatal oxidative stress, and reduced neuronal injury and pyknosis in the substantia nigra, accompanied by an increased number of TH-positive neurons. Re A restored striatal dopamine and its metabolite levels, activated the PI3K/Akt pathway, and upregulated TH protein expression. In vitro, Re A alleviated rotenone-triggered cytotoxicity and oxidative stress, reversed the suppression of PI3K/Akt signaling, and elevated TH expression. These protective effects were partially abolished by LY294002. Rehmannioside A exerts neuroprotective activity against rotenone-induced PD lesions, possibly via activating the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, suppressing oxidative stress and preserving dopaminergic function. Re A may serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for PD.

title: A systematic review on the possible role of microRNA-155 in cancer treatment.
abstract: Overexpression of microRNA-155 (miR-155) has been associated with cancer development, metastasis, and possible drug resistance. This systematic review analyzed the evidence from the existing literature on miR-155 expression in cancer patients undergoing treatment. A thorough literature search was conducted in databases and search engines (ProQuest, PubMed, and Google Scholar) from January 2019 to December 2024 to identify clinical evidence on miR-155 expression in cancer treatments. To assess miR-155 expression in relation to clinical outcomes, we included 15 cancers in this systematic review. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, three independent reviewers selected, extracted, and assessed the data against the predefined inclusion criteria, and a fourth reviewer verified the assessments and resolved discrepancies. Of the 15 cancers analyzed, 19 eligible studies covering eight cancers were identified and included in the review, namely breast cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia, cutaneous melanoma, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, papillary thyroid cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Screening and evaluation of these 19 studies showed that miR-155 expression varied by cancer type, treatment strategy, and patient sample type. While most studies associated miR-155 overexpression with treatment resistance, a few reported an association between elevated miR-155 expression and enhanced treatment sensitivity. A limitation of this study is that the search for studies reporting miR-155 expression in relation to therapeutic outcomes in patients with cancer was restricted to three databases and a 5-year timeframe. Overall, the results of this study indicate that the prognostic and predictive significance of miR-155 warrants further evaluation. PROSPERO ID, CRD42025632573.

title: Clinical value evaluation of MEG3/miR-144-3p as a biomarker for the early diagnosis of glaucoma.
abstract: LncRNA MEG3 and miR-144-3p have been confirmed to be related to ocular pathological processes, but their roles as early diagnostic biomarkers for Primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) and the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. The targeting relationship between MEG3 and miR-144-3p was verified by the dual luciferase reporter gene assay. MEG3 and miR-144-3p expression were detected by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). ROC curves and correlation analysis were used to evaluate the diagnostic value and correlation of MEG3 and miR-144-3p. NaIO3 was used to treat retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), CCK-8 was used to measure cell proliferation and survival rate, and ELISA was used to detect levels of CAT, MDA, and inflammatory factors (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β). MEG3 and miR-144-3p have a targeting relationship. Compared with the healthy control group, the expression of MEG3 in tears and serum of patients with early POAG was significantly increased, while the expression of miR-144-3p was decreased. ROC analysis showed that MEG3 (serum AUC = 0.899; tears AUC = 0.894) and miR-144-3p (serum AUC = 0.877; tears AUC = 0.873) had excellent diagnostic efficacy for early POAG. In RGCs, silencing MEG3 or overexpressing miR-144-3p could alleviate NaIO3-induced cell damage, inflammation, and oxidative stress. MEG3 and miR-144-3p form a regulatory axis involved in glaucoma pathogenesis. Their abnormal expression in tears and serum makes them promising non-invasive biomarkers for early POAG diagnosis. The aqueous humor samples used in the study were solely for the analysis of the correlation of regulatory mechanisms.

title: The rise of super-emotional intelligence.
abstract: The debate about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) runs along a single axis: cognitive capability and its projected culmination in superintelligence. We argue that this framing leaves a complementary axis unexamined and propose the goal of Super-Emotional Intelligence (SEI): systems that perceive, model, regulate, and respond to affect better than skilled human experts, while remaining human-centered. SEI is a performance construct realized by a functional architecture, not a claim about machine experience, and we give measurable criteria for each of its four capacities. Today's affect-aware AI, from multimodal emotion recognition to empathic chatbots, recognizes, or simulates emotion at or below human level and is judged against human ceilings. Three things would set SEI apart: perception that adds peripheral and contactless physiological channels, none of them emotion-specific, but some, like the vestigial ear muscles, resolving affective processing at the timescale of the events that evoke it; a generative model of affect grounded in active inference rather than pattern matching; and functional allostatic self-regulation. The decisive gap in current systems is architectural. A sensed state conditions a prompt, but nothing carries a state estimate across turns, models the effect of the system's own responses, or selects actions under an explicit objective. We specify such a closed loop, state the conditions under which it is stable and steerable rather than manipulative, propose a preregistered validation plan whose failure would falsify our claims, and treat governance as a design constraint of the loop rather than an afterthought.

title: Integrated computational screening and biochemical validation identify natural small molecules targeting Aβ aggregation and dissociation.
journal: Journal of pharmacy & pharmaceutical sciences : a publication of the Canadian Society for Pharmaceutical Sciences, Societe canadienne des sciences pharmaceutiques
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ), a pathological hallmark implicated in disease onset and progression. Aβ undergoes self-assembly from monomers into soluble oligomers, protofibrils, insoluble fibrils, and extracellular plaques. Our previous studies have shown that Jowiseungchungtang, which consists of 14 medicinal herbs, inhibits Aβ aggregation and ameliorates Aβ-mediated pathology in AD models. However, the active small molecules underlying these effects remain unidentified. To identify small molecules from these 14 medicinal herbs, we constructed a library of 1,751 compounds and applied an integrated in silico and in vitro workflow. First, these 1,751 compounds were filtered based on drug-likeness and predicted blood-brain barrier permeability, yielding 566 candidates. Second, molecular docking of 566 selected compounds against Aβ conformers identified five candidates predicted to interact with aggregation-prone residues critical for Aβ aggregation and fibril stabilization. Third, Thioflavin T assays demonstrated that four compounds-1-monopalmitin, isobutyl octyl oxalate, pentadecanoic acid, and dimethyl azelate-significantly inhibited Aβ42 aggregation. Additionally, isobutyl octyl oxalate and pentadecanoic acid disaggregated preformed Aβ42 aggregates. Fourth, molecular dynamics simulations were performed to examine the short-timescale behavior of the candidate compounds with the Aβ17-42 dimer, showing transient ligand-Aβ interactions associated with structural rearrangements at the dimer interface. Pharmacokinetic predictions supported drug-likeness, showing blood-brain barrier permeability and systemic clearance. Collectively, these findings identify four Jowiseungchungtang (JWS)-derived candidate compounds with Aβ aggregation-inhibitory activity and provide a mechanistic and pharmacokinetic basis for further development of these compounds as potential therapeutic agents in AD.

title: Trauma and posttraumatic growth in cancer: validation of the post-traumatic stress disorder checklist for DSM-5 and the posttraumatic growth inventory-short form in patients with breast cancer.
abstract: Cancer diagnosis is a stressful event that may trigger post-traumatic stress (PTS) symptoms, while also fostering positive psychological changes known as post-traumatic growth (PTG). Although distinct, PTS and PTG often co-occur among women with breast cancer. Despite their clinical relevance, validated self-report measures of PTS and PTG remain limited in oncology. This study validated the Portuguese versions of the Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and the Posttraumatic Growth Inventory - Short Form (PTGI-SF) in women with breast cancer. A total of 122 women with early-stage breast cancer completed both scales at 12 and 18 months after diagnosis, considering the cancer experience as the traumatic event. Cross-sectional analyses, including confirmatory factor analyses, internal consistency estimates, and construct validity correlations, used the 12-month assessment. Test-retest reliability was examined between the 12- and 18-month assessments. Construct validity was examined with the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule - Short Form (PANAS-SF) and the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30). The PCL-5 demonstrated excellent four-factor fit, high internal consistency, and generally acceptable test-retest reliability, although reliability was poor for the Avoidance subscale. Convergent validity was supported by positive correlations with negative affect (PANAS-SF), and divergent validity by negative correlations with positive affect (PANAS-SF) and quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30). The PTGI-SF showed a good fit to a unidimensional model, with excellent internal consistency (α = 0.91; ω = 0.91) and high test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.91), although correlations with affect and quality of life were non-significant, indicating limited convergent and divergent validities. Overall, findings support the psychometric adequacy of the PCL-5 and, to a lesser extent, the PTGI-SF, in patients with breast cancer and low PTS symptom levels. The PCL-5 appears robust for assessing PTS symptoms in this population, while the PTGI-SF captures global growth experiences, despite weaker evidence for validity. Combined use of both instruments may provide a comprehensive assessment of vulnerability and resilience following breast cancer, supporting more individualized psychosocial care and guiding future research on psychological responses to cancer, including larger and more clinically diverse samples, as patients with higher PTS symptom severity.

title: Automated temporal analysis reveals stress-induced protracted feeding regulated by mesolimbic dopamine in mice.
abstract: Feeding behavior is altered in neuropsychiatric disorders, and environmental stressors also shape it. In our previous study, mice exposed to multiple stressors developed feeding behavior patterns characterized by a deviated bait approach, which we defined as "fixated feeding," together with impairment of the mesolimbic dopamine system. Here we examined the temporal organization of feeding behavior using an AI-based analytical framework built on DeepLabCut and SimBA. Mice subjected to social isolation or intermittent high-fat diet (HFD) exposure showed prolonged feeding bouts, a pattern we define as "protracted feeding." Dopamine administration into the nucleus accumbens (NAcc) shell attenuated diet- and isolation-induced protracted feeding. Physical restraint stress alone did not induce protracted feeding, but mosapride treatment prolonged feeding bouts in restrained mice. Restraint-associated peripheral autonomic and gastrointestinal states may therefore influence the expression of stress-related temporal feeding deviations. In the VTA-DREADD cohort, the same temporal analysis showed that inhibition of VTA dopaminergic activity prolonged feeding bouts. This extends the fixated-feeding circuit framework from the spatial to the temporal domain. These deviations were not consistently accompanied by changes in the amount consumed or in metabolic factors, so alterations in temporal feeding patterns may reflect perturbation of a stress-associated pathway in the mesolimbic dopamine system. Protracted feeding, together with fixated feeding, may serve as a candidate behavioral readout of stress-associated reward-system dysfunction.

title: Adjunctive extracorporeal shock wave therapy after botulinum toxin type A injection for post-stroke spasticity: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
abstract: Post-stroke spasticity is a common rehabilitation problem, and botulinum toxin type A (BTX-A) is a standard focal treatment. Whether extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) provides clinically relevant additional benefit after BTX-A remains uncertain. This systematic review and three-level meta-analysis evaluated the add-on effect of ESWT after BTX-A for post-stroke spasticity, with particular attention to impairment-level and activities-of-daily-living outcomes. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, VIP, and CBM were searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials of BTX-A plus ESWT in adult post-stroke spasticity were included. The primary quantitative synthesis was restricted to BTX-A-based comparators. Hedges' g was pooled with three-level random-effects models to account for dependent effect sizes. Seven randomized controlled trials with 377 participants met the qualitative criteria, and six trials with 242 participants contributed to the primary quantitative synthesis. Adjunctive ESWT was associated with greater reduction in Modified Ashworth Scale scores (g = 0.87, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.34; p < 0.001) and greater improvement in Fugl-Meyer Assessment scores (g = 1.11, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.76; p < 0.001). Activities-of-daily-living estimates favored the combined intervention but did not reach conventional statistical significance (g = 1.15, 95% CI -0.03 to 2.32; p = 0.056). Two participants developed transient erythema after ESWT, but adverse-event reporting was too incomplete for a comparative safety estimate. Adjunctive ESWT may improve short-term impairment-level outcomes after BTX-A, but certainty is limited and evidence for reliable functional independence gains is very uncertain. Modality-, target-, timing-, and dose-specific findings remain exploratory. Identifier INPLASY202630010; https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.3.0010.

title: Case Report: Neurosurgery, octreotide, cabergoline, radiotherapy, pasireotide and pegvisomant - a multimodal strategy for adolescent acrogigantism.
abstract: Growth hormone (GH)-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs) are rare in the pediatric population. They often present as large, invasive tumors and are frequently associated with an underlying genetic predisposition, making their management particularly challenging. Optimal treatment requires an individualized multidisciplinary approach, which often involves a combination of surgery and adjuvant medical therapy or radiotherapy when necessary. We present a challenging case of an adolescent female with acrogigantism. The patient was diagnosed at the age of 13 years and 10 months during the evaluation of chronic headaches. Brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed an invasive PitNET measuring 38 × 23 × 32 mm, while biochemical assessment confirmed marked GH hypersecretion. The disease followed an aggressive course, and biochemical control could not be achieved despite optimal multimodal therapy. Sequential treatment included neurosurgical resection, octreotide LAR, cabergoline, pasireotide LAR, proton beam radiotherapy, and pegvisomant. Combination therapy with pegvisomant and octreotide LAR ultimately normalized insulin-like growth factor 1 concentrations while maintaining long-term radiological tumor stability. This case underscores the complexity of managing aggressive GH-secreting PitNETs in adolescents and emphasizes the need for individualized, multidisciplinary care and long-term follow-up. Combined medical therapy with pegvisomant and octreotide LAR may provide effective biochemical control when surgery, radiotherapy, and standard medical treatment are insufficient.

title: Investigating cardiorespiratory fitness, cerebral blood flow, and brain metabolism in epilepsy.
abstract: Idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) are characterized by seizures that propagate through widespread thalamocortical networks including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Poor cardiorespiratory fitness may exacerbate neurovascular and metabolic vulnerability including heightened susceptibility to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. We aimed to examine cardiorespiratory fitness, regional cerebral blood flow (CBF), and metabolite concentrations in patients with IGEs (PwIGEs) and to determine the effect of seizure control status on these physiological and neurochemical measures. Forty-six participants (31 PwIGEs, 15 healthy controls) underwent a graded exercise test to assess maximal oxygen uptake (VO2peak) as a measure of cardiorespiratory fitness and completed 3T MRI including multi-delayed pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) to assess CBF and single-voxel spectroscopy (SVS) to assess ratios of N-acetylaspartate and glutamate/glutamine complex to total creatine (NAA/tCr and Glx/tCr, respectively) in the ACC and thalamus. Group differences and seizure control effects in PwIGEs were examined using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). VO2peak, thalamic CBF, ACC NAA/tCr, and ACC Glx/tCr did not significantly differ between groups. PwIGEs exhibited higher ACC CBF (p = 0.039) and lower thalamic NAA/tCr (p = 0.012) than healthy controls. PwIGEs with active seizures showed significantly lower thalamic Glx/tCr compared to those who were seizure-free (p = 0.003). These findings suggest poor cardiorespiratory fitness is not epilepsy-specific and likely attributable to lifestyle and that region-specific alterations in perfusion and metabolic milieu in PwIGEs characterized by higher ACC CBF and lower thalamic NAA/tCr and Glx/tCr in those with active seizures. The multimodal neuroimaging approach provides convergent evidence of thalamocortical network dysregulation underlying IGE pathophysiology.

title: Expert Review on the Use of Methylphenidate in Children and Adult With Epilepsy and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder.
abstract: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a comorbidity affecting 12%-29% of individuals with epilepsy, significantly impacting learning, psychosocial development, behaviour, and quality of life. Moreover, ADHD and epilepsy share a bidirectional relationship. Although methylphenidate has been proven effective in alleviating ADHD symptoms, its use remains limited in individuals with epilepsy due to outdated concerns-dating back over 20 years-that psychostimulants could increase seizure frequency. This manuscript presents a narrative review of the scientific literature published between January 2000 and May 2026 regarding the use of methylphenidate in patients with epilepsy and ADHD. Based on the available evidence, a panel of paediatric neurologists from five Spanish tertiary hospitals with expertise in epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders reached an expert consensus and developed a series of practical recommendations for the assessment and management of these patients. This expert group issued several recommendations, including the proactive screening of ADHD symptoms in all children and adults with epilepsy from the onset of the condition. Current evidence has not consistently demonstrated an increased seizure risk associated with methylphenidate in patients with epilepsy, although available data remain limited for some epilepsy subgroups. Furthermore, undertreatment of ADHD is associated with poorer patient outcomes. Methylphenidate may be considered in children and adults with epilepsy when clinically indicated, following optimization of epilepsy management, associated comorbidities, and behavioural and psychosocial interventions. Treatment decisions should be individualized, particularly in patients with active epilepsy, drug-resistant epilepsy, recent seizure worsening, or developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.

title: Exploration of various administration routes for the nitric oxide donating organic nitrite, nitrosooxypropanol, in a porcine model.
abstract: Organic nitrites are restricted to intravenous or inhaled administration. The aim was to explore novel administration routes for an organic nitrite, previously demonstrated to have pulmonary selectivity, in normal and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Hemodynamic and respiratory variables, including fraction of exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), were measured in 13 anesthetized pigs. In naïve conditions, nitrosooxypropanol (PDNO) was given subcutaneously (100-1600 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose, 30 min interval), intramuscularly (50-400 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose, 30 min interval), intravenously (5-80 nmol/kg/min; 30 min infusion), intranasally (500-2000 nmol/kg boli), and sublingually (80-16,240 nmol/kg boli). In pulmonary hypertension (intravenous infusion of U46619), PDNO was given intravenously (5-45 nmol/kg/min; 15-20 mins infusion/dose) and subcutaneously (200-1800 nmol/kg/min; 5 min/dose at 20 min interval). Recovery was calculated using FeNO. PDNO, given by all administration routes, dose-dependently decreased systemic blood pressure and increased FeNO. Subcutaneous and intramuscular administration induced slow-onset (9 min to maximum effect) and long-lasting effects (~30 min). Intravenous administration induced rapid effects (1-2 min to steady state) and prompt decline after infusion cessation. The proportion of PDNO reaching exhaled gas (intravenous administration as reference; FeNO-based recovery) was 17% (intramuscularly) and 9% (subcutaneously). In pulmonary hypertension, intravenous and subcutaneous administration decreased the pulmonary/systemic vascular resistance-ratio. In this exploratory proof-of-concept study evaluating novel administration routes for organic nitrites, PDNO demonstrated measurable biological effects and acceptable FeNO-based recovery following intramuscular and subcutaneous administration. Furthermore, intranasal and tentatively sublingual administration showed biological effects. Future work on formulation and investigations into relevant disease models is warranted.

title: Progressive Lineage Restriction of Bergmann Glia-Like Progenitors During Postnatal Cerebellar Development.
abstract: Bergmann glia-like progenitors (BGLPs) are transient progenitors in the postnatal cerebellum, but how their lineage potential changes during development remains incompletely understood. Our previous electroporation-based study suggested that P0 BGLPs possess broader lineage potential than P6 BGLPs. Here, we performed recombination-based lineage tracing by cerebellar surface application of tamoxifen to Ai9/+; GlastCreERT2/+ mice and temporally analyzed the progeny of BGLPs labeled at P0, P3, P6, and P8. We found that BGLPs undergo progressive lineage restriction during postnatal development. P0 BGLPs gave rise to Bergmann glial cells (BGs), inner granule cell layer astrocytes (IGL astrocytes), white matter astrocytes (WM astrocytes), and molecular layer inhibitory neurons (ML-INs), confirming our previous electroporation-based findings. In contrast, P3 BGLPs generated BGs, IGL astrocytes, and WM astrocytes, whereas P6 BGLPs generated BGs and IGL astrocytes, and P8 BGLPs generated predominantly BGs. Thus, BGLP lineage output was progressively restricted from four progeny categories at P0 to a predominantly BG-restricted output by P8, suggesting that BGLPs dynamically adjust their cellular output during postnatal cerebellar maturation. Additional temporal analyses were consistent with a stepwise pathway from P0 BGLPs to ML-INs, in which astrocyte-like progenitors (AsLPs) appear first among BGLP descendants, some of which may subsequently transition into committed inhibitory neuron progenitors (INPs) that give rise to ML-INs. These findings identify postnatal BGLPs as a useful in vivo model for studying progressive lineage restriction and stage-specific cellular supply during cerebellar development.

title: Brain Mechanisms Linking Type 2 Diabetes to Alzheimer Disease: A Multimodal Imaging Framework.
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer disease and cognitive impairment; however, the mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. Here, we propose and justify a mechanistic, multimodal imaging framework to examine how type 2 diabetes-associated hyperglycemia and neurovascular dysfunction may contribute to cognitive vulnerability and accelerated brain aging. Dynamic metabolic stress testing using multimodal glucose-challenge imaging methods is proposed as the central component of this framework to investigate cerebral blood flow, blood-brain barrier integrity, metabolic demand, functional connectivity, and structural brain alterations under conditions of acute hyperglycemia. By examining these complementary neurovascular and metabolic responses together, rather than as individual imaging measures, this proposed approach is intended as a mechanistic discovery platform to identify neurovascular pathways linking type 2 diabetes mellitus-related dysglycemia with cognitive vulnerability in a population with a high burden of metabolic risk. By integrating current mechanistic evidence with a proposed multimodal imaging approach, this work aims to generate testable mechanistic hypotheses and inform future biomarker-driven and longitudinal studies of diabetes-related dementia risk.

title: Impact of nano-chitosan solution on psoriasis-like thin skin lesion induced by imiquimod in Wistar rats: Exploring novel epigenetic role targeting miR-155, JAK2/STAT3/RORC/IL-17A, and MyD88/NF-κB pathways.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated skin disorder manifested by keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Current therapies provide symptomatic relief but carry the risk of severe side effects. Chitosan, a natural biopolymer, has wound-healing and anti-inflammatory properties in various dermatological applications. This study aimed to assess the impact of chitosan solution on psoriasis-like skin lesions induced by imiquimod (IMQ) in a Wistar rat model. An IMQ-induced psoriatic skin lesion was induced in Wistar rats; 35 rats were divided equally into: Control, IMQ, IMQ + acetic acid, IMQ + chitosan (5 g/L), and IMQ + chitosan (10 g/L) groups. Macroscopic, histopathological, immunohistochemical, biochemical, and molecular analyses were conducted to assess morphological and structural alterations, inflammatory responses, oxidative stress markers, and gene expression profiles. Application of IMQ resulted in psoriatic-like morphological and histopathological skin alterations. Chitosan application ameliorated these alterations and significantly reduced the erythema, desquamation, and skin thickening. Histological evaluation revealed that chitosan solution reduced epidermal acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, and inflammatory infiltrates while improving dermal architecture. It also suppressed PCNA and S100 expression, markers for keratinocyte proliferation and inflammation, respectively. Biochemically, it reduced IL-6, p-JAK2, p-STAT3, IL-17A, MyD88, and NF-κB levels, while restoring redox balance by decreasing MDA and enhancing catalase activity. Furthermore, qRT-PCR analysis demonstrated chitosan-mediated downregulation of miR-155 and RORC, highlighting its immunomodulatory effect. Nano-Chitosan solution effectively mitigated IMQ-induced psoriasis-like skin lesions, with better efficacy for the higher dose, through cytoprotective, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunoregulatory mechanisms. It has the ability to target the JAK2/STAT3/RORC/IL-17A and MyD88/NF-κB pathways via downregulating miR-155, which reveals a novel molecular mechanism for chitosan's beneficial effects and suggests its potential as an alternative therapeutic strategy for psoriasis.

title: [Methylphenidate-induced liver damage].
abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is liver damage caused by medicines and accounts for approximately 15% of all cases of liver failure. Psychotropic drugs account for a significant proportion of the above group of medicines. The clinical presentation can range from an asymptomatic mild elevation of liver enzymes to severe hepatitis. We discuss the case of a 22-year-old patient who presented at a follow-up appointment at a psychiatric outpatient clinic with asymptomatic liver damage, one week after starting treatment with methylphenidate. A review of the literature shows that this rare side effect is caused by an idiosyncratic, dose-independent pathological mechanism in which the metabolism of methylphenidate plays a significant role. Blood tests at the start of treatment are recommended for early detection, particularly in high-risk patients.
keywords: Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury

title: [Xanomeline-trospium: A review of clinical studies in patients with schizophrenia].
abstract: Xanomeline-trospium (KarXT) is a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist that was approved in the United States in 2024 for the treatment of people with schizophrenia. This medication represents a novel mechanism of action within antipsychotic pharmacotherapy. To provide an overview of clinical studies evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of xanomeline-trospium in adults with schizophrenia. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase and PsycInfo up to 30 January 2026. Randomised controlled clinical trials and post hoc analyses of xanomeline-trospium in adults with schizophrenia were included. All included studies were required to be registered in international trial registries to be eligible for inclusion. The primary outcome was change in total PANSS score. Three randomised, placebo-controlled phase 2 or 3 studies (n = 690) each demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in psychotic symptoms with xanomeline-trospium compared with placebo (PANSS difference −8 to −12 points). Adverse effects mainly consisted of transient peripheral cholinergic effects such as gastrointestinal complaints. Sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms, weight gain and prolactin elevation did not occur more frequently than with placebo. Efficacy for negative and cognitive symptoms was not convincingly demonstrated. Xanomeline-trospium is an effective and generally well-tolerated antipsychotic with a novel mechanism of action. However, its definitive place in treatment remains unclear due to the lack of direct comparisons with existing antipsychotics, limited data on efficacy in treatment-resistant patients, and the absence of long-term outcome data. Further research is required to determine potential effects on negative and cognitive symptoms.

title: [Intermetamorphosis after subdural haematoma: a familiar face, different identity].
abstract: A 78-year-old female patient developed a delusion following drainage of a right-sided subdural haematoma: she believed that her husband was her deceased father. The clinical presentation was consistent with a misidentification syndrome. In such syndromes, there is a fixed belief that a person, place, or object has a different identity or meaning. In this case, the phenomenon concerned intermetamorphosis, a subtype of misidentification syndromes. In intermetamorphosis, an individual is perceived as having completely transformed into another person: the physical appearance remains unchanged, but the identity is experienced as different. Treatment with olanzapine resulted in complete remission without recurrence. This case highlights the importance of early recognition of misidentification syndromes within neuropsychiatric and geriatric practice. Based on previous publications in the Nederlands Tijdschrift voor Geneeskunde and the Tijdschrift voor Psychiatrie, we outline diagnostic approaches and treatment options for misidentification syndromes.

title: Nanoplastics-induced neurotoxicity: neurovascular dysfunction, cognitive impairment, and mechanisms of cell death.
abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are increasingly recognized as environmentally persistent contaminants capable of reaching the central nervous system (CNS), yet the mechanistic basis linking brain exposure to cognitive dysfunction remains incompletely resolved. Emerging evidence indicates that NPs can cross or perturb the blood-brain barrier (BBB), accumulate within neural tissues, and interact with neurons, microglia, astrocytes, neural progenitors, and cerebrovascular cells. These interactions have been associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, synaptic injury, and disruption of hippocampal homeostasis, although the strength and causal nature of evidence for individual mechanisms vary across experimental models. Importantly, regulated cell death (RCD) is emerging as a critical mechanistic bridge between cellular toxicity and neurocognitive outcomes, encompassing apoptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and cuproptosis. However, evidence for specific cell-death pathways remains largely based on molecular and cellular signatures in experimental models, and oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, or altered expression of pathway-associated proteins alone should not be considered definitive evidence of pathway activation. Recent studies further implicate microglial extracellular traps, excessive mitochondrial fission, and glymphatic dysfunction as potentially important pathways connecting NP exposure with neuronal injury and cognitive decline. Environmental co-exposures may intensify these effects, highlighting the context-dependent nature of NP neurotoxicity. This review integrates current evidence linking NP exposure to cognitive and behavioral abnormalities, emphasizing the interconnected roles of neurovascular dysfunction, glial-neuronal crosstalk, oxidative-mitochondrial stress, synaptic disruption, RCD, and impaired brain clearance mechanisms.

title: Spatial heterogeneity of the tumor immune microenvironment in gastric cancer: exploratory associations with clinicopathological features.
abstract: We aimed to describe the spatial heterogeneity of selected immune-cell populations and stromal markers within the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) of gastric cancer and to explore their associations with clinicopathological features. CD8, CD20, CD163, FOXP3, PD-1, and SMA were assessed by immunohistochemistry in 102 resected gastric cancer specimens. Positive cells were quantified, and SMA was semi-quantitatively scored, in the tumor center (TC), inner invasive margin (IIM), and outer invasive margin (OIM). Exploratory clustering of CD8/CD20-enriched and CD163/FOXP3-enriched cell proportions was used to define exploratory TIME pattern groups (CD8/CD20-enriched, CD163/FOXP3-enriched, and intermediate); heterogeneity grades were based on group consistency across regions. Associations with clinicopathological features and survival were analyzed. CD163+ macrophage-like cells predominated, but their proportion decreased from TC to OIM (p < 0.001), whereas the proportion of CD20+ B cells increased (p < 0.001). Moderate/high heterogeneity was observed in 69% of cases. In the OIM, the distribution of exploratory TIME pattern groups was associated with lymph node metastasis, deeper invasion, and advanced TNM stage (all p < 0.001), but survival differences were not statistically significant. PD-1+ cell density peaked in the OIM (p < 0.001), and the PD-1/CD8 ratio was higher in both TC and OIM than in IIM. In the OIM, the CD8/CD20-enriched pattern had the highest PD-1+ cell density and the CD163/FOXP3-enriched pattern the lowest (p < 0.05), with no significant differences in TC and IIM. SMA+ stromal scores decreased from TC to OIM, were highest in the CD163/FOXP3-enriched pattern, and were inversely associated with CD8+ T cell and CD20+ B cell densities. In conclusion, gastric cancer exhibits a structured, non-random spatial immune microenvironment, with the TC and invasive margins representing immunologically distinct compartments. PD-1 expression and stromal components show region-specific features within this spatial immune landscape. These findings reveal exploratory associations with clinicopathological features and provide a basis for further validation in independent cohorts.

title: The Relationship between Cortical GABA Levels and Short-Interval Intracortical Inhibition: A Meta-analysis of Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Studies.
abstract: Cortical gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the brain's principal inhibitory neurotransmitter and plays a key role in regulating motor cortical excitability. Short interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), measured via paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), is a widely used physiological index of GABAergic function. However, the strength and consistency of the association between GABA levels, quantified in vivo using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), and SICI remain unclear across studies. We conducted a random-effects meta-analysis of studies reporting correlations between MRS-derived cortical GABA concentrations and TMS-measured SICI in healthy human participants. Effect sizes were transformed to Fisher's Z scores and pooled using the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) method. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic and Cochran's Q test. Potential publication bias was evaluated via visual funnel plot inspection and Egger's regression test. Results: A total of 23 effect sizes were included in the analysis. The pooled Fisher's Z was -0.14 (95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02; P = .03), corresponding to a small but statistically significant negative correlation (r ≈ -0.14). This finding suggests that higher cortical GABA levels are modestly associated with stronger intracortical inhibition. Heterogeneity was low to moderate (I² = 35.5%; Q = 34.73; P = .04). Funnel plot inspection revealed mild asymmetry, but Egger's test showed no significant smallstudy effects (β₁ = -0.46; P = .58), indicating minimal publication bias. This meta-analysis provides quantitative evidence supporting an inverse association between cortical GABA concentrations and SICI, reinforcing GABA's role in modulating intracortical inhibition. While the effect size is modest, the findings appear robust and consistent. Future research should employ standardized acquisition and reporting protocols and explore the clinical relevance of this relationship in populations with disrupted GABAergic signaling.

title: Gut-Induced Synuclein Propagation: A New Mechanism in Neurodegenerative Disease.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
