abstract: Gut-induced synuclein propagation has emerged as a potential mechanism linking gastrointestinal disturbances with the development and progression of Parkinson disease and related synucleinopathies. These disorders are characterized by progressive accumulation and spreading of misfolded α-synuclein (α-Syn), leading to selective neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although traditionally considered brain-centered diseases, increasing evidence indicates that gastrointestinal abnormalities, peripheral α-Syn pathology, and gut-associated immune alterations may precede neurological manifestations, suggesting that peripheral processes can influence disease evolution. Here, we review clinical, pathological, and experimental evidence supporting the role of intestinal environmental stress, microbial dysregulation, barrier dysfunction, and immune activation in promoting α-Syn misfolding, aggregation, and transmission through interconnected pathways. However, peripheral α-Syn abnormalities alone are unlikely to be sufficient to initiate neurodegeneration, indicating the presence of additional biological constraints. We propose a cumulative-threshold and biological-gates framework in which α-Syn induction, seed formation, propagation efficiency, anatomical connectivity, and neuronal vulnerability collectively determine whether gut-associated pathology progresses into a self-sustaining neurodegenerative cascade. Understanding the determinants that enable gut-induced synuclein propagation may provide new insights into disease heterogeneity and guide biomarker development and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for synucleinopathies.

title: Tractography-Based Insights into Neuroplasticity and Clinical Heterogeneity in Parkinson's Disease Subtypes.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
abstract: Parkinson's disease shows substantial heterogeneity across motor, cognitive, and non-motor domains, reflecting variable patterns of neurodegeneration and compensation across distributed brain circuits. Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) tractography enables pathway-specific characterization of white-matter alterations and provides a framework for linking clinical subtypes to tract-level patterns that may be obscured by skeleton-based or connectomic averaging. Here, we synthesize white-matter evidence across motor, cognitive, genetic, and prodromal dimensions of PD heterogeneity, using tractography as an organizing framework within a broader dMRI and multimodal context. We review diffusion approaches ranging from diffusion tensor imaging to free-water, neurite, and fixel-based models. We distinguish pathway reconstructions from other diffusion and imaging analyses and consider how complementary approaches inform, but do not uniquely determine, interpretations of degeneration and subtype-specific neuroplasticity. Emerging methods, including harmonization pipelines, radiomic tractometry, and machine learning classifiers, may further improve tract-level sensitivity and reproducibility. Cognitive subtypes illustrate how posterior association and limbic tract degeneration, together with cholinergic and noradrenergic dysfunction, shape clinical progression. Integrating tractography with molecular, genetic, functional, and clinical markers may support subtype-specific biomarkers for risk stratification, prognosis, and targeted neuromodulation or rehabilitation strategies, although longitudinal and external validation is required before routine use.

title: A Delphi-Based Item Set for Pre-Test Asthma Probability Assessment in Children Undergoing Methacholine Challenge Test.
abstract: To select, through a Delphi consensus process, the clinical items most relevant to pre-test probability of asthma (PTPA) in children undergoing methacholine challenge test (MCT) and to explore their association with expert-estimated PTPA. Delphi-selected items are associated with PTPA estimated independently by pediatric pulmonologists. Three-round e-Delphi, followed by a retrospective analysis of item association with expert-estimated PTPA. A database of 92 children referred for MCT at a tertiary center. A steering committee proposed 11 candidate items, rated by 23 experts (consensus threshold ≥ 80%). Five pediatric pulmonologists, blinded to MCT results and not involved in the Delphi, independently estimated PTPA from clinical history. Agreement was assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Associations between retained items and mean PTPA were assessed using a multivariable linear regression. Ten items were retained (nine reached consensus; pneumonia/atelectasis was retained by steering-committee judgment). Single-rater ICC was 0.78 (95% CI 0.70-0.85); average-measures ICC was 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97). Multivariable linear regression retained all ten items; each positively associated with PTPA. The strongest associations were seen with wheezing after age 3 years (β 15, 95% CI 7.4-23), wheezing within the last 3 years (β 14, 95% CI 6.4-22) and complete response to anti-asthma treatment with relapse after treatment cessation (β 34, 95% CI 27-41). Delphi consensus identified ten clinically relevant items, all associated with expert-estimated PTPA. As the outcome was expert judgement rather than confirmed asthma, diagnostic value remains unestablished; outcome-based studies are needed.

title: Effects of Maternal Ligature-Induced Periodontitis on Brain in Offspring.
abstract: The combined effects of chronic maternal periodontitis on offspring gut microbiome and brain outcomes remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of maternal oral microbiome disruption on brain function and gut microbiome in offspring. Periodontitis was induced in 11- to 12-wk-old parous C57BL/6J mice by maintaining ligatures around both sides of the maxillary second molars for 4 wk, followed by breeding with naïve male mice. Maternal oral and gut microbiome, as well as the offspring gut microbiome, was analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Male offspring were evaluated at 7 to 8 wk of age via a set of analyses, including behavioral tests, microbiome profiling, RNA sequencing, immunohistochemistry for glial cell populations, and in vivo calcium imaging. Cerebellar DNA methylation was assessed at embryonic day 18.5 to examine early epigenetic alterations. Maternal periodontitis significantly reduced microbial diversity in the maternal oral microbiome and altered the composition of the maternal gut microbiome. In offspring, α-diversity was reduced in the gut microbiome. Behavioral analyses revealed impaired social interaction and reduced spontaneous locomotion, while motor coordination and memory-related behaviors were preserved. RNA sequencing identified region-specific changes in gene expression, particularly in the cerebellum, highlighting its vulnerability to maternal inflammatory conditions. DNA methylation analysis revealed epigenetic alterations during the fetal stage, suggesting early programming effects. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated a significant increase in astrocyte density in the cerebellum and frontal cortex, whereas oligodendrocytes and microglia were unaffected. Furthermore, calcium imaging revealed disrupted neuronal synchrony among Purkinje cells without significant changes in individual neuronal activity parameters. Maternal oral microbiome disruption induces coordinated alterations in maternal and offspring microbiomes and leads to persistent neurobehavioral, molecular, and cellular changes in offspring. These findings provide new insights into the link between maternal oral health and offspring neurodevelopment, highlighting the potential role of microbiome-mediated mechanisms in shaping brain function.

title: Sex differences in parietal alpha power during sustained attention are related to conflict monitoring performance in mild cognitive impairment.
abstract: BackgroundSex differences in cognition among individuals with dementias and prodromal stages such as amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) manifest in variations in severity and prevalence, but underlying brain activity patterns remain unclear. This study is a secondary endpoint study of the Cogmax project.ObjectiveWe examined sex differences in parietal alpha power during an attention task (Simple Vigilance Task, SVT) and its association with conflict monitoring (Stroop Color-Word Test Part 3, T score) in individuals with aMCI.MethodsThe SVT served as the EEG recording condition because of its low cognitive demands and visually driven structure, while the Stroop task provided an independent neuropsychological measure of conflict monitoring. Seventy-seven participants (23 females; 54 males) were included. We analyzed average power spectral density (PSD) across occipital and parietal electrodes (O1-Pz-O2-P7-P8) using multitaper Fourier transform. Normalized alpha power was calculated as integrated 7-11 Hz relative to total 0.1-40 Hz PSD.ResultsAll participants showed high accuracy on the SVT, indicating stable attentional engagement. Covariate-adjusted permutation tests, robust to unbalanced sample sizes, showed that females exhibited higher parietal alpha power and higher Stroop Part 3 T-scores than males. However, when Stroop performance was included as a covariate, the sex difference in alpha power became nonsignificant. A positive correlation between Stroop 3 scores and parietal alpha power was observed in females but not in males, suggesting a sex-specific relationship.ConclusionsParietal alpha activity may be associated with conflict monitoring performance in aMCI, particularly among females, providing evidence for sex-related neural differences in aMCI.

title: Short-term gepant use during active cluster headache bouts: A consecutive case series.
journal: Cephalalgia : an international journal of headache
abstract: AimTo evaluate the short-term effectiveness and tolerability of gepants administered during active cluster headache (CH) bouts in routine clinical practice, focusing primarily on reduction in daily attack frequency and additionally on pain intensity, bout duration, and patient-reported outcomes.MethodsWe conducted an observational, uncontrolled, consecutive case series at a reference headache clinic. Patients fulfilling ICHD-3 criteria for episodic or chronic CH who initiated a standardized 28-day course of a gepant during an active bout between October 2024 and July 2025 were included. Baseline data were abstracted from clinical records and diaries. No systemic corticosteroids, greater occipital nerve blocks, preventive dose adjustments, or new preventives were introduced during the 28-day period. The primary endpoint was ≥50% reduction in mean daily attack frequency at the end of treatment compared with baseline. Secondary outcomes included change in pain intensity (Numerical Rating Scale, NRS), change in attack duration, impact on overall bout duration, Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC), and adverse events. Analyses were descriptive.ResultsTen patients were included (seven episodic CH [ECH], three chronic CH [CCH]). Median baseline attack frequency was three attacks/day (range 1-6), and median baseline NRS was 8.5. The primary endpoint was achieved in 7/10 patients (70.0%): 5/7 with ECH (71.4%) and 2/3 with CCH (66.7%). Two ECH patients with a low baseline frequency (two attacks/day) did not meet the ≥50% criterion but demonstrated marked reductions in pain intensity and shortened bout duration. Overall, pain intensity improved in 9/10 patients (90.0%), with a median NRS reduction of 7 points (range 0-10). Median intensity reduction was greater in ECH (7 points; range 2-10) than in CCH (2.5 points; range 0-5). Shortening of individual attacks was reported in 4/10 (40.0%), and reduction in overall bout duration in 7/10 (70.0%), predominantly among ECH. Median time to perceived benefit was 96 h. Adverse events were mild (nausea or constipation in 2/10).ConclusionIn this small real-world case series, short-term gepant use during active cluster bouts was associated with multidimensional clinical improvement, particularly in episodic CH. Benefits extended beyond attack frequency to include substantial reductions in pain intensity and apparent modulation of bout duration. Given the uncontrolled design and limited sample size, findings should be interpreted cautiously but support further prospective, phenotype-stratified investigation.

title: Discrimination of Synthetic and Natural Caffeine by Carbon and Nitrogen Stable Isotope Ratio Analysis Utilizing GC-C-IRMS.
journal: Rapid communications in mass spectrometry : RCM
abstract: Caffeinated drinks and supplements are popular products, many of which claim to use naturally derived caffeine. The availability of less expensive synthetic caffeine can motivate adulteration. Additionally, the caffeine content of these products can be inaccurately labeled, raising health concerns. As a result, effective testing methods are required to distinguish synthetic and natural caffeine and to test caffeine content in complex matrixes. In this study, a stable isotope method for natural caffeine authentication is described and applied to commercial samples. The accuracy of labeled caffeine content of products is evaluated. Samples containing exclusively natural caffeine (i.e., coffee, tea, guarana, yerba mate) and synthetic caffeine were selected. Commercial products claiming to contain natural caffeine including supplements, energy drinks, and guarana products were also tested. Caffeine was extracted by incubation with a water-ammonium hydroxide mixture and phase separation with dichloromethane. Its carbon and nitrogen stable isotope composition was determined using GC-C-IRMS. Caffeine content was determined by HPLC-DAD. Natural and synthetic caffeine could be distinguished, with some limitations, based on carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) isotopes. Based on this distinction, 15 of the 75 commercial samples labeled as containing natural caffeine were adulterated. The rate of apparent adulteration was high in guarana products (~78%) and supplements (~22%). Caffeine content deviating from label claim by more than ±20% was observed in 46% of the 86 samples tested, ranging from 57% to 217% of the labeled content. Carbon and nitrogen isotope ratio analysis by gas chromatography-combustion-isotope ratio mass spectrometry is an efficient method for distinguishing natural and synthetic caffeine in commercially available products. Such testing is important given the significant number of apparently mislabeled products on the USA market. The prevalence of inaccurate caffeine content labeling may raise health concerns, highlighting the need for better production quality control and increased testing.

title: Neural connectomes of verbal fluency in post-stroke aphasia.
journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
abstract: Verbal fluency tasks are widely used to assess language abilities and executive functions in both clinical and research settings. In post-stroke patients, prior research has indicated a significant hodological contribution to the neural basis of verbal fluency; however, this has largely been examined using lesion-based measures, predefined tractography approaches, and traditional diffusion metrics. Quantitative anisotropy-based structural connectometry derived from correlational tractography was employed to determine the white matter circuits underlying semantic and phonemic fluency in 44 patients with post-stroke aphasia. Both task types were found to be linked to anterior frontal connections of left-hemisphere dorsal and ventral associative pathways, as well as domain-general projection pathways. However, visual inspection of the connectomes, supported by supplementary cross-control analyses, suggested differences in the relative emphasis and distribution of pathways, with phonemic fluency aligning more with the dorsal stream, while semantic fluency showed greater reliance on the ventral stream and a wider range of cortico-subcortical connections. The findings contribute to current understanding of the neural networks of verbal fluency in aphasia, with potential relevance for clinical practice and research.

title: Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure model of osmotically-driven cytoplasmic flow in severed axons.
abstract: Repair (sealing) of traumatic plasmalemmal lesions involves the formation, movement, and accumulation of vesicles at the injury site by active transport and by passive bulk flow of cytoplasm. We show that hypotonic and hypertonic salines affect the direction and rate of vesicle movement in severed crayfish medial giant axons (CMGAs), presumably because osmotically-driven changes in intracellular pressure alter bulk cytoplasmic flow along the axon and at the lesion site. We develop a general Hagen-Poiseuille pressure-cable biophysical model of bulk cytoplasmic flow to predict direction and relative rate of cytoplasmic influx and efflux for CMGAs and other axons modeled as fluid-filled cylinders with distributed osmotic water permeability. Although our general-model applies to axons of any length, this model simplifies for a short-cable model in which the axonal length is much shorter than the hydraulic length constant, i.e., axons like CMGAs. Both General- and Shortcable-Models predict that hypotonic extracellular conditions drive transmembrane water flux into an axon, elevating intracellular pressure that is relieved by cytoplasmic efflux at the injury site. Conversely, hypertonic conditions drive transmembrane water flux out of the axon that is relieved by extracellular fluid influx at the severed end. Our data from CMGAs show that active transport involving molecular motors associated with microtubules and actin in CMGAs is the predominant contributor to vesicle movement towards severed end. Bulk cytoplasmic flow - as assessed by the movement of vesicles and cellular debris that persist when active transport is inhibited - is a lesser contribution to vesicle movement whose extent depends on the difference between extracellular and intracellular osmolarity. Our Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure Model accurately predicts the direction and approximate rate of movement of vesicles and cellular debris under all osmotic conditions tested. Our Model should also account for vesicle behavior in other axons and cylindrical cytoplasmic processes of various diameters and lengths.

title: Top-Down Self-Regulation: Bidirectional Associations Between Vagal Regulation and Cool and Hot Executive Functions in Adolescents.
abstract: Vagal regulation and executive functions both reflect top-down self-regulation. However, how vagal regulation and executive functions are interconnected with each other during adolescence remains an open question. This study investigated bidirectional associations between vagal regulation and cool and hot executive functions in adolescents using a two-wave data collection (T1: November 2021, T2: May 2023). At both waves, 163 Chinese adolescents (Mage = 12.92, SDage = 0.82; 47.24% females) underwent a speech task during which their baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and RSA suppression were obtained, assessing vagal regulation, and completed a Flanker task and an Emotional Stroop task, assessing cool and hot executive functions, respectively, indexed by intra-individual reaction time variability. Results showed that baseline RSA was not significantly associated with either cool or hot executive functions at T1 or T2. Additionally, RSA suppression to the impromptu speech task was bidirectionally associated with hot executive functions across timepoints, while unidirectionally associated with cool executive functions, with only the predicted direction from RSA suppression to cool executive functions being found. Findings revealed distinct prospective associations between vagal regulation and hot and cool EFs, providing a possibility for further investigation of longitudinal co-development of different aspects of top-down self-regulation during adolescence. SUMMARY: This study is the first to explore the bidirectional associations between vagal regulation and executive functions (EFs) as two aspects of top-down self-regulation. No significant associations between baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and cool and hot EFs were found. RSA suppression to the impromptu speech task was bidirectionally associated with hot EFs and unidirectionally associated with cool EFs during adolescence. Findings revealed distinct prospective associations between vagal regulation and hot and cool EFs.

title: Lower recorded prevalence of Alzheimer's disease in natalizumab-exposed older adults with multiple sclerosis: A hypothesis-generating observation.
abstract: Adaptive immune mechanisms, including CD8 T cell-mediated neuroinflammation, are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We examined whether exposure to natalizumab, an α4-integrin antagonist that restricts leukocyte trafficking into the central nervous system, was associated with Alzheimer's disease prevalence among older adults with multiple sclerosis. Using Epic Cosmos electronic health record data, we identified 875,226 individuals with MS, of whom 9095 had an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis after age 65 years. Alzheimer's disease prevalence differed significantly across disease-modifying therapies, with natalizumab-treated patients demonstrating the lowest prevalence (0.13%; 95% confidence interval: 0.10-0.17%). These findings demonstrate a lower recorded prevalence of late-life Alzheimer's disease among natalizumab-exposed patients; however, given the aggregated nature of the data, this observation should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

title: Handedness literacy in teachers: Data from Greece, Serbia, and Belgium.
abstract: Handedness literacy, a term coined here to refer to one's knowledge about and understanding of handedness, is an understudied yet crucial component of educational neuroscience. It is distinct from attitudes toward left-handers, but it can inform the practical and psychosocial support teachers provide to their left-handed students, thereby promoting better classroom ergonomics and reducing stigma. This study investigated teachers' handedness literacy for the first time, focusing on educators from Greece (n = 273), Serbia (n = 365), and Belgium (n = 213). Qualitative responses from Greek and Serbian educators differed in emphasis (neurobiological versus practical), but generally revealed supportive attitudes towards left-handers. Quantitative analysis from all three countries highlighted factual misunderstandings, with many educators incorrectly associating left-handedness with increased intelligence, or expressing substantial uncertainty about whether left-handedness is a feature of autism and dyslexia. Contrary to our hypothesis, left-handed educators did not demonstrate superior handedness literacy compared to their right-handed counterparts. Additionally, teachers across countries consistently overestimated the proportion of left-handers in the population, possibly conflating left-handedness with general non-right-handedness. Most teachers further acknowledged the need for improved handedness literacy. Findings underline the critical importance of integrating formal training about handedness into teacher education and professional development programs.
